lessons.title: The system design interview framework
lessons.summary: A repeatable 45-minute structure for backend design rounds: requirements, estimation with real numbers, API, data model, high-level design, deep dives and trade-offs.
lessons.body:
## What the round is really testing
A backend system design interview gives you a vague product ("design Twitter", "design a rate limiter") and 45-60 minutes. There is no single right answer. The interviewer is watching how you turn ambiguity into a concrete, defensible design: whether you ask the right questions, size the problem with numbers, pick storage that fits the access patterns, and reason about failure and trade-offs under follow-up pressure.

It is closer to a design review with a senior colleague than an exam. You lead; they steer. A common failure is the "box recital": drawing load balancer, cache, Kafka and Cassandra in the first five minutes without ever saying why. Another is going so deep on one component that you never finish an end-to-end design.

## The structure
Use the same skeleton every time and say it out loud at the start. It shows you have a plan and lets the interviewer redirect you cheaply.

| Step | Output on the board | Rough time (45 min) |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Requirements | Functional list, non-functional targets, out of scope | 5-7 min |
| 2. Estimation | QPS, storage, bandwidth, memory: only numbers that matter | 3-5 min |
| 3. API | 3-6 endpoints or events with key fields | 3-5 min |
| 4. Data model | Entities, keys, partition key, chosen store | 4-6 min |
| 5. High-level design | 6-10 boxes, the read path and the write path traced | 8-10 min |
| 6. Deep dives | 2-3 hard parts, chosen with the interviewer | 12-15 min |
| 7. Wrap-up | Bottlenecks, failure modes, what you would do next | 2-3 min |

Many people compress 3 and 4, or do estimation after the API. That is fine. What matters is that requirements come first and deep dives get real time.

## Step 1: requirements
Split them into two lists and write both down.

**Functional**: the 3-5 user-visible capabilities that are in scope. For a chat app: 1:1 messages, group chats up to N members, delivery and read receipts, online presence, history sync across devices. Then explicitly park things: "out of scope: voice calls, end-to-end encryption key management, search." Writing out-of-scope items is a signal of maturity, and it gives the interviewer a chance to say "actually, I want you to cover search."

**Non-functional**: the qualities that drive architecture.
- **Scale**: DAU, peak factor, read/write ratio, data growth.
- **Latency**: targets per path, usually as a percentile ("p99 redirect under 50 ms").
- **Availability**: 99.9% is about 43 minutes of downtime a month, 99.99% about 4.3 minutes. Say which paths need which.
- **Consistency**: where is stale data acceptable (feed, like counts) and where is it not (payments, inventory)?
- **Durability**: can we ever lose a write? Messages and payments: no. View counters: occasionally fine.

If the interviewer says "you decide", state an assumption with a number and move on. Silence while you deliberate costs more than an imperfect assumption.

## Step 2: back-of-envelope estimation
Estimation is not arithmetic theatre. Each number should feed a decision: do we need sharding, does the hot set fit in memory, is bandwidth the real cost, can a single primary take the writes?

Useful constants to have in your head:

```text
1 day            = 86,400 s  ~ 10^5 s  (use 10^5 for speed)
1 month          ~ 2.5 x 10^6 s
1 year           ~ 3 x 10^7 s
1 million / day  ~ 12 per second
Peak             ~ 2-3x average (more for spiky events)

Sizes:   1 KB = 10^3 B, 1 MB = 10^6, 1 GB = 10^9, 1 TB = 10^12, 1 PB = 10^15
Latency (orders of magnitude, from Jeff Dean's list):
  main memory reference          ~100 ns
  read 1 MB sequentially, memory ~ a few microseconds to ~250 us (era-dependent)
  SSD random read                ~ 16-150 us
  round trip within a datacenter ~ 0.5 ms
  round trip US coast to coast   ~ 40-70 ms; transatlantic ~ 80-150 ms
```

The exact latency values have shifted since Jeff Dean's original list (the gist by Jonas Bonér is the common reference); what matters in an interview is the ratios: memory is roughly 1000x faster than a network hop in the same datacenter, and a cross-continent round trip is tens of milliseconds you cannot engineer away.

### A worked example: 100 million DAU social app
Assume each user views their feed 10 times a day and posts once every 5 days, average post 1 KB of text plus metadata, 20% of posts include a 500 KB image.

```text
Reads:   10^8 users x 10 views     = 10^9 feed reads/day
         10^9 / 10^5 s             = ~10^4 QPS average, ~3 x 10^4 peak
Writes:  10^8 / 5                  = 2 x 10^7 posts/day
         2 x 10^7 / 10^5           = ~200 writes/s average, ~600 peak
Ratio:   ~50:1 read heavy  -> caching and precomputation pay off

Text storage per day:  2 x 10^7 x 1 KB    = 20 GB/day  -> ~7 TB/year
Images per day:        4 x 10^6 x 500 KB  = 2 TB/day   -> ~730 TB/year
                       -> object storage + CDN, not the database

Feed egress:  3 x 10^4 peak QPS x 20 posts x 1 KB = ~600 MB/s of JSON at peak
```

Conclusions you say out loud: writes are trivially small for a sharded store; reads dominate, so precomputed feeds and caching matter; images dominate storage and bandwidth, so they go to object storage behind a CDN and never through the API servers. That is three design decisions from two minutes of maths.

Skip numbers that change nothing. If the whole dataset is 50 GB, say "fits on one primary with replicas; I won't shard for size" and move on.

## Step 3: API
Write the external contract before drawing internals. It forces precise thinking about what the system actually does.

```text
POST /v1/posts                 { text, mediaIds[] }         -> 201 { postId, createdAt }
GET  /v1/feed?cursor=&limit=20                              -> { posts[], nextCursor }
POST /v1/posts/{id}/likes      Idempotency-Key header       -> 204
WS   /v1/stream                server pushes { type: "new_post", postId }
```

Things interviewers notice: cursor pagination instead of offsets for anything that changes under you; idempotency keys on mutating calls that clients retry; auth (the user id comes from the token, never from the body); and whether real-time delivery is a push channel or polling.

## Step 4: data model
List entities with their primary key and the queries they must serve. The **access pattern decides the store**, not fashion.

```text
users      (user_id PK, handle UNIQUE, created_at, ...)
posts      (post_id PK, author_id, created_at, text, media[])   query: by author, newest first
follows    (follower_id, followee_id, created_at)               query: followers of X, followees of X
timelines  (user_id, post_id, score)                            query: top N for user
```

Then say how you would partition: posts by `author_id` keeps "a user's posts" on one shard; follows stored twice (by follower and by followee) so both directions are single-partition reads. This is the moment to discuss SQL vs a wide-column store: relational for transactions and flexible queries at moderate scale; a wide-column or key-value store when the access pattern is "fetch by key, sorted by time" at very high write volume (Discord's move from Cassandra to ScyllaDB for messages is a well-documented example).

## Step 5: high-level design
Draw the minimum set of boxes that serves every functional requirement, then trace a write and a read through it.

```text
            clients (web, iOS, Android)
                     |
                  CDN (static, media)
                     |
              L7 load balancer / API gateway  (TLS, auth, rate limits)
                     |
     +---------------+----------------+
     |               |                |
 post service   feed service    media service --> object storage
     |               |                               (S3-like)
     v               v
 posts DB       timeline cache  <-- fan-out workers <-- queue (Kafka)
 (sharded)      (Redis)                                  ^
     |                                                   |
     +-------------- post created event -----------------+
```

Narrate it: "A post write goes to the post service, which stores it and emits an event; fan-out workers push the post id into followers' cached timelines; a feed read hits the timeline cache and hydrates post bodies from a post cache." Every box should have a reason to exist. If you cannot explain why the queue is there, remove it.

## Step 6: deep dives
This is where most of the signal is, especially for senior levels. Pick 2-3 topics that are genuinely hard for this product, and ask the interviewer which they prefer. Typical menu:
- **Scaling the hot path**: caching strategy, hot keys, sharding and rebalancing.
- **Consistency**: what happens on concurrent writes, read-your-own-writes, ordering.
- **Failure**: a node dies, a region goes down, the queue backs up. What degrades, what is lost?
- **The product-specific problem**: celebrities in a feed, matching in Uber, idempotency in payments, transcoding in video.

For each deep dive use a mini-structure: the problem, two or three options, the trade-off table in words, your choice, and how it fails.

## Trade-offs: how to talk about them
Every interesting decision has a cost. Strong candidates say it before being asked:
- "I'm caching timelines in Redis. The cost is memory, roughly 800 post ids per active user, and staleness of a few seconds, which this product accepts."
- "I'm choosing at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers rather than trying for exactly-once, because exactly-once across a network is really deduplication anyway."
- "Async fan-out means a new post can take a few seconds to appear for followers. If the product needs instant, we'd pay for it with synchronous writes on the post path."

The Google SRE book's chapter on cascading failures is worth reading for the failure-mode vocabulary: overload, retries amplifying load, and load shedding.

## How interviewers score it
Rubrics at large companies differ in wording but share axes:

| Axis | Weak signal | Strong signal |
|---|---|---|
| Problem exploration | Starts drawing immediately | Scopes, quantifies, states assumptions |
| Design quality | Boxes without reasons | Simple design that meets requirements, traced end to end |
| Technical depth | Buzzwords ("use Kafka") | Explains partitioning, consistency, failure behaviour |
| Trade-offs | One option presented as obvious | Alternatives compared against requirements |
| Communication | Monologue or silence | Checks in, adapts when steered |

Level calibration matters. A mid-level candidate is expected to produce a working, reasonable design. A senior candidate is expected to drive, find the hardest problems unprompted, and discuss operations: rollout, monitoring, failure handling, cost. Staff-level answers add organisational and evolutionary concerns: how the system changes over two years, which parts are bets.

## Common mistakes
- **Solving at Google scale when 1,000 QPS was the requirement.** Over-engineering is as bad as under-engineering.
- **Estimation that leads nowhere.** Five minutes of numbers and no conclusion.
- **No read/write path walkthrough.** The interviewer cannot tell if the design actually works.
- **Naming technology instead of properties.** "Cassandra" is not an answer; "a store partitioned by user id with time-sorted clustering, tolerant of eventual consistency" is, and then you can name an example.
- **Ignoring failure.** What happens when the cache is cold, the queue lags, or a shard is down?
- **Not managing time.** Glance at the clock at each transition.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** whether you can scope, whether your numbers lead to decisions, whether your design works end to end, and how you react when they push on a weak point.

**Model 60-second opening:**
1. "Let me confirm the core use cases and the scale, then I'll do quick estimates, sketch the API and data model, draw a high-level design and spend the second half on the hardest parts."
2. Ask 4-6 targeted questions, write functional and non-functional lists, park the rest.
3. Estimate QPS, storage and the hot set; draw one conclusion from each.
4. API and data model with partition keys.
5. Boxes, write path, read path.
6. "The interesting problems here are X and Y. Which would you like me to go deeper on?"

**Follow-ups to expect:** "What if traffic grows 10x?", "Where is the single point of failure?", "What happens when this component is down?", "How would you monitor this?", "What would you build first with a team of three?"
keyPoints: Spend the first 5-8 minutes on functional and non-functional requirements; write explicit out-of-scope items so the interviewer can redirect early.
Estimate only what changes the design: QPS (peak, read/write split), storage over years, bandwidth and memory for the hot set. 1 day is roughly 10^5 seconds.
Define the API and data model before drawing boxes; access patterns decide the database and the partition key.
Draw the simplest working design first, then spend half the round on 2-3 deep dives the interviewer cares about.
Every choice is scored as a trade-off: name the alternative, why you rejected it, and the failure mode of what you picked.
interview: How do you structure a 45-minute backend system design interview?
Walk me through a back-of-envelope estimate for a service with 100 million daily active users.
What separates a senior system design answer from a mid-level one?

check.q: A service has 100 million DAU and each user makes 10 reads per day. What is the average read QPS, roughly?
check.why: 10^8 users x 10 reads = 10^9 reads per day. Divided by about 10^5 seconds per day gives about 10^4, roughly 11,600 QPS average. Peak is usually 2-3x that.

check.q: When is it reasonable to skip a detailed storage estimate in a design round?
options: Never, every number must be computed
When you plan to use a NoSQL database
When the data obviously fits on one machine and storage does not drive any decision
check.why: Estimation exists to drive decisions such as sharding, caching or tiering. If the total is a few hundred GB, say so in one line and move on.

check.q: What is the most common reason strong engineers fail system design rounds?
options: Jumping into components before agreeing on requirements and then running out of time for depth
Not knowing the exact latency of an L1 cache hit
check.why: Without scoped requirements the design solves the wrong problem, and without time management there is no time for the deep dives that carry most of the senior signal.

lessons.title: Design a URL shortener
lessons.summary: The classic warm-up design: key generation without collisions, a read path that serves redirects from cache in milliseconds, 301 vs 302, analytics and abuse.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
A URL shortener maps a short code to a long URL: `sho.rt/aZ3kQ9x` redirects to `https://example.com/some/very/long/path?utm=...`. Underneath, it is a key-value store with two operations: create a mapping (rare) and resolve a code (very frequent). The interview is a warm-up, but it hides three real problems: generating unique codes cheaply, serving redirects with very low latency at high read volume, and counting clicks without slowing the redirect.

Interviewers use it to see whether you can run the full framework on a small problem and still find depth: key generation, caching, HTTP semantics and abuse.

## Requirements
**Functional**
- Create a short link for a long URL; optionally a custom alias and an expiry.
- Redirect a short code to the long URL.
- Per-link click analytics (counts over time, referrer, country).
- Out of scope unless asked: user accounts beyond an API key, link editing, QR codes.

**Non-functional**
- Redirect p99 under about 50 ms at the server (users perceive a redirect as part of page load).
- High availability on the read path; creating links can degrade a little.
- Codes must never collide and ideally should not be trivially enumerable.
- Durable: a created link must keep working for years.

## Estimation
Assume 100 million new links per month and a 100:1 read to write ratio.

```text
Writes:   10^8 / (2.5 x 10^6 s)          = ~40 creates/s average, ~100-200 peak
Reads:    40 x 100                       = ~4,000 redirects/s average, ~10-20k peak
Storage:  10^8 links/month x 12 x 5 years = 6 x 10^9 links
          x ~500 B (code, URL, metadata)  = ~3 TB over 5 years
Code space: 6 x 10^9 needed; base62^7 = 3.5 x 10^12  -> 7 chars is plenty
Cache:    links follow a power law. Caching the hottest ~20% of a day's
          traffic: 4,000/s x 10^5 s x 0.2 x 500 B = ~40 GB  -> fits a small Redis cluster
```

Conclusions: writes are tiny (one database could take them); reads are moderate but latency-sensitive, so cache aggressively; 3 TB is too much for a comfortable single node over time, so plan to partition by code.

## API

```text
POST /v1/links
  Authorization: Bearer <api key>
  Idempotency-Key: <uuid>
  { "url": "https://...", "alias": "launch-2026"?, "expiresAt": "..."? }
  -> 201 { "code": "aZ3kQ9x", "shortUrl": "https://sho.rt/aZ3kQ9x" }

GET /{code}
  -> 302 Location: https://...        (or 404 / 410 Gone if expired)

GET /v1/links/{code}/stats?from=&to=&granularity=day
  -> { "clicks": [...], "topReferrers": [...], "countries": [...] }
```

The idempotency key matters: a mobile client that times out and retries should not create two codes for the same request.

## Data model

```text
links
  code        PK  (string, 7 chars)
  long_url        (text, validated, max ~2-8 KB)
  owner_id
  created_at
  expires_at      (nullable)

click_events (append-only, to a log / warehouse, not the OLTP store)
  code, ts, referrer, country, user_agent_class

click_rollups
  (code, day) PK -> count
```

The only hot query is `get by code`, which is a pure key lookup. That fits a key-value or wide-column store (DynamoDB, Cassandra) partitioned by `code`, or a relational database sharded by hash of `code`. PostgreSQL is perfectly reasonable at this scale with a few shards; say so rather than reaching for a NoSQL store by reflex.

## High-level design

```text
                 client / browser
                       |
           +-----------+------------+
           |                        |
     GET /{code}               POST /v1/links
           |                        |
   edge / CDN (optional cache   API gateway (auth, rate limit)
   of 302s with short TTL)          |
           |                  link service ---- ID range allocator
   redirect service                 |           (DB sequence / ZooKeeper / etcd)
     |       |                      v
     |   Redis cache  <------  links DB (sharded by code, replicated)
     |   (code -> url)
     |
     +--> click log (Kafka / Kinesis) --> stream aggregator --> rollups DB
                                      \-> object storage / warehouse
```

**Write path**: authenticate, validate the URL (scheme allow-list, length, safe-browsing check), obtain a code, insert `code -> url` with a uniqueness constraint, return. Optionally write through to the cache.

**Read path**: look up the code in Redis; on a miss read a replica of the links DB and populate the cache; respond with a redirect; emit a click event to the log without waiting for acknowledgement beyond the local buffer. The redirect service is stateless and horizontally scaled.

## Deep dive 1: generating codes
This is the question interviewers push on. Three families:

**1. Hash the URL** (MD5/SHA-256, take the first 7 base62 characters). Deterministic, so the same URL maps to the same code, which can be nice. But truncation causes collisions; with billions of links the birthday bound makes them certain, so you need a check-and-retry (append a salt, rehash). And two users shortening the same URL would share a code, which breaks per-user analytics unless you hash `url + user`.

**2. Random codes.** Generate 7 random base62 characters (from a CSPRNG), insert with a unique constraint, retry on conflict. At 6 billion used out of 3.5 trillion, the conflict probability per insert is about 0.2%, so retries are rare. Simple and not enumerable. Cost: every write needs a uniqueness check, which is cheap with a primary key.

**3. Counter plus base62 encoding.** A global integer counter, encoded in base62. Never collides, no check needed. A single counter is a bottleneck, so use **range leasing**: each link-service instance asks the allocator for a block (say 10,000 IDs), then mints locally. The allocator can be a database sequence incremented by the block size, a Redis `INCRBY`, or a ZooKeeper/etcd node. A crashed server loses its unused range, which is harmless. Twitter's Snowflake is a related approach: 64-bit IDs from timestamp, worker id and sequence, no coordination per ID.

```ts
const ALPHABET = "0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ";

export function toBase62(n: bigint): string {
  if (n === 0n) return "0";
  let out = "";
  while (n > 0n) {
    out = ALPHABET[Number(n % 62n)] + out;
    n /= 62n;
  }
  return out;
}

class RangeAllocator {
  private next = 0n;
  private end = 0n;
  constructor(private lease: (size: bigint) => Promise<bigint>, private size = 10_000n) {}

  async nextId(): Promise<bigint> {
    if (this.next >= this.end) {
      const start = await this.lease(this.size); // e.g. Redis INCRBY returns the new end
      this.next = start - this.size;
      this.end = start;
    }
    return this.next++;
  }
}
```

Sequential codes are enumerable: anyone can walk `aZ3kQ9x`, `aZ3kQ9y` and scrape every link. If links may be private, either use random codes or permute the counter through a reversible bijection (for example a small Feistel network or multiplying by a large odd constant modulo 62^7) so consecutive IDs look unrelated. That keeps the no-collision property and hides the order.

**Custom aliases** share the namespace: insert with the same unique constraint; reserve words like `api`, `admin`, `login`; and ensure generated codes cannot collide with aliases (for example, different length or a prefix rule).

## Deep dive 2: 301 vs 302 vs 307
- **301 Moved Permanently**: browsers and proxies may cache it indefinitely. Repeat visits skip your service entirely: less load, lower latency, but you lose click analytics and cannot change or disable the link for those clients.
- **302 Found / 307 Temporary Redirect**: not cached by default; every click hits you. 307 guarantees the method is preserved, which matters only for non-GET requests.
- A middle ground: 302 with `Cache-Control: private, max-age=300` lets a browser reuse the redirect for a few minutes.

Bitly-style products that sell analytics use non-permanent redirects. State the trade-off explicitly; interviewers love this question because it connects HTTP semantics to a business requirement.

## Deep dive 3: the read path at scale
- **Cache**: `code -> url` in Redis with an LRU or LFU policy. Hit rates above 90% are realistic because of the power-law popularity. Negative caching (store "not found" for a minute) blocks scanners hammering random codes.
- **Hot keys**: a link going viral can push one key to tens of thousands of requests per second. An in-process LRU in each redirect instance (a few seconds TTL) absorbs that before it reaches Redis.
- **Edge**: for global latency, serve redirects from edge functions or CDN caches near users. A 302 with a short `s-maxage` can be cached at the CDN while still counting clicks via CDN logs.
- **Database**: reads go to replicas; the dataset is partitioned by hash of code so no shard gets the "newest" codes all at once (range partitioning on sequential codes would create a hot shard).

## Deep dive 4: analytics without slowing redirects
Never increment a counter row synchronously on every click. Instead, append a click event to a log (Kafka, Kinesis) or to a local buffer that flushes in batches. A stream processor (Flink, Kafka Streams, or a simple consumer) aggregates per code per minute and upserts rollups. Raw events land in object storage for ad-hoc analysis. Losing a few clicks during a crash is usually acceptable; say so, it is a requirement decision.

## Abuse and safety
Shorteners are used for phishing and malware. Check new URLs against a safe-browsing list, rate-limit creation per API key and IP, allow only `http`/`https` schemes (never `javascript:`), and support takedown: a disabled link returns 410 and is purged from caches. Note how a 301 makes takedown impossible for clients that cached it.

## Trade-offs and common mistakes
- Choosing a hash and forgetting collisions.
- A single global counter with no range leasing: a bottleneck and single point of failure.
- Range-partitioning sequential codes and creating a hot shard.
- Writing analytics synchronously on the redirect path.
- Over-engineering: at 40 writes per second, a distributed consensus system per write is unnecessary.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** code generation and collisions, cache design and hit rate, 301 vs 302, sharding key choice, and whether analytics is decoupled.

**60-second outline:** scope (create, redirect, analytics, expiry); estimate (~40 writes/s, ~4k reads/s, ~3 TB over 5 years, 7-char base62); API (POST links with idempotency key, GET code returns 302); data model keyed by code; design (stateless redirect service, Redis cache, sharded DB, click log to aggregator); deep dive on code generation via leased counter ranges with an optional bijection, then caching and hot keys.

**Follow-ups to expect:** "How do you stop enumeration?", "What if a link goes viral?", "How would you make redirects fast globally?", "How do you delete expired links?" (TTL index or background sweeper plus cache purge), "What happens if the ID allocator is down?" (servers keep minting from their current lease; leases are large enough to ride out a short outage).
keyPoints: It is a read-heavy key-value lookup: 100:1 reads to writes is a typical assumption, so the redirect path must be served from cache or an edge.
Base62 with 7 characters gives 62^7, about 3.5 trillion codes; the hard part is generating them without collisions or coordination on every write.
Counter-based IDs (ranges handed out per server) avoid collisions without a lookup; hashing needs collision checks; random codes need a unique constraint and retry.
301 lets browsers cache the redirect forever and hides clicks from analytics; 302 or 307 keeps every click visible at the cost of more traffic.
Click analytics must be asynchronous (log or queue to an aggregator) so the redirect never waits on a write.
interview: Design a URL shortener like bit.ly.
How do you generate short codes without collisions at scale?
Should a URL shortener return 301 or 302, and why does it matter?

check.q: Roughly how many distinct codes does a 7-character base62 alphabet allow?
check.why: 62^7 is about 3.52 x 10^12. Six characters give about 5.7 x 10^10 (57 billion), eight about 2.2 x 10^14.

check.q: Why do many designs hand out ID ranges (for example blocks of 1,000 counter values) to each app server?
options: So each server can mint unique codes locally without a network call per write
check.why: A central counter hit on every write is a bottleneck and single point of failure. Leasing ranges amortises coordination: one call per thousand codes, and a crash only wastes the unused part of a range.

check.q: The product team wants an accurate click count per link. Which redirect status is the better default?
check.why: Browsers may cache a 301 indefinitely and stop contacting the shortener, so repeat clicks are invisible. A 302/307 sends every click through the service, where it can be counted.

lessons.title: Design a news feed (Twitter / Instagram home timeline)
lessons.summary: Fan-out on write vs fan-out on read, the celebrity problem and the hybrid that solves it, timeline caches, hydration and how ranking changes the design.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
A home feed shows a user recent (or relevant) posts from the accounts they follow. The interesting part is not storing posts; it is assembling a personalised list quickly for hundreds of millions of users, where the follow graph is extremely skewed. Most accounts have a few hundred followers; a handful have tens of millions.

There are two basic strategies:
- **Fan-out on write (push)**: when someone posts, insert the post id into every follower's precomputed timeline. Reading is a single lookup.
- **Fan-out on read (pull)**: store posts per author; at read time, fetch recent posts from everyone the user follows and merge them.

Martin Kleppmann uses exactly this example in the first chapter of *Designing Data-Intensive Applications*, based on Twitter's 2012 numbers: read traffic was two orders of magnitude higher than write traffic, so Twitter moved to fan-out on write, then had to treat celebrities differently.

## Requirements
**Functional**: post (text, media), follow/unfollow, home timeline (reverse chronological first, ranked as an extension), user timeline (a user's own posts).
**Out of scope**: search, trends, DMs, ads, notifications (mention them as separate systems).

**Non-functional**: timeline load p99 under ~200 ms server-side; a new post visible to followers within a few seconds (eventual consistency is fine); very high availability for reads; the posting user must see their own post immediately (read-your-own-writes).

## Estimation
Assume 300 million DAU, each opens the feed 5 times a day, 20% of DAU post once a day, average 200 followers per poster.

```text
Feed reads:   3 x 10^8 x 5 / 10^5 s       = 15,000 QPS avg, ~45,000 peak
Posts:        6 x 10^7 / 10^5 s           = 600 posts/s avg, ~2,000 peak
Fan-out:      600 posts/s x 200 followers = 120,000 timeline inserts/s avg
              (peaks and celebrities push this much higher)
Timeline cache: keep 800 ids x 8 bytes = ~6.4 KB per user
              x 3 x 10^8 active users     = ~2 TB raw; with Redis overhead
              plan for several TB -> sharded cache cluster, active users only
Posts storage: 6 x 10^7 x 1 KB/day = 60 GB/day, ~22 TB/year (text + metadata)
```

The 800-entry cap echoes Twitter's 2012 talk, where home timelines in Redis were capped at roughly that size. Conclusion: fan-out is the dominant write load, timeline storage is large but affordable if limited to active users, and reads must be served almost entirely from memory.

## API

```text
POST /v1/posts                    { text, mediaIds[] }       -> { postId }
GET  /v1/timeline/home?cursor=&limit=20                      -> { items[], nextCursor }
GET  /v1/users/{id}/posts?cursor=&limit=20
POST /v1/users/{id}/follow        DELETE /v1/users/{id}/follow
```

Cursor is an opaque encoding of the last post id or score seen. Offsets break as new posts arrive at the head.

## Data model

```text
posts       post_id (Snowflake-style: time-sortable 64-bit), author_id, created_at, text, media
            partition by author_id or post_id; query "posts by author, newest first"
follows     stored twice: by follower (who do I follow) and by followee (who follows me)
            followee -> followers list is what fan-out reads; can be millions long
home_tl     Redis sorted set or list per user: user_id -> [post_id ...] capped at ~800
post_cache  post_id -> post object; user_cache: user_id -> profile; counters separately
```

Time-sortable ids (Snowflake puts a millisecond timestamp in the high bits) let you sort timelines by id instead of storing a separate timestamp, and let the cursor be just an id.

## High-level design

```text
 client
   |
 API gateway ---------------------------------+
   |                                          |
 post service --> posts DB (sharded)      timeline service
   |                                       |        |
   +--> "post_created" event (Kafka)       |   home timeline cache (Redis, sharded by user)
              |                            |        ^
        fan-out workers ------------------+--------+   (push ids into followers' lists)
              |  reads follower lists from graph service / follows store
              |
        skip followers who are inactive; skip authors flagged "celebrity"

 timeline read: timeline cache ids  +  celebrity posts pulled  -> merge -> hydrate
                                                                  (post cache, user cache,
                                                                   counters, viewer's like state)
```

**Write path**: the post service persists the post, then publishes an event. Fan-out workers page through the author's follower list and append the post id to each follower's timeline (Redis `LPUSH` + `LTRIM`, or `ZADD` + `ZREMRANGEBYRANK`). The author's own timeline is updated synchronously so they see their post at once.

**Read path**: read the cached id list, merge in pulled celebrity posts, take the top N, hydrate in batch (multi-get from post and user caches), filter (deleted posts, blocked users, muted words), return with a cursor.

## Deep dive 1: push vs pull vs hybrid

| | Fan-out on write | Fan-out on read |
|---|---|---|
| Write cost | O(followers) per post | O(1) |
| Read cost | O(1) lookup | O(followees) queries + merge |
| Freshness | Delay = fan-out time | Always fresh |
| Wasted work | Fan-out to users who never log in | None |
| Bad case | Celebrities | Users following thousands |

**Hybrid** is the standard answer and what Twitter described: push for most authors; for accounts above a follower threshold (say 100k-1M), skip fan-out and pull their recent posts at read time. Each user follows only a handful of celebrities, so the read-time merge is small: fetch "recent posts by these 5 authors" from a per-author cache and merge with the precomputed list.

Two more optimisations:
- **Skip inactive users.** Do not fan out to users who have not logged in for 30 days; rebuild their timeline on demand (pull) when they return.
- **Prioritise fan-out**: process posts from accounts with fewer followers first, so a celebrity's job does not delay everyone else.

## Deep dive 2: the celebrity problem in detail
A 50-million-follower account under pure push means 50 million cache writes per post. At, say, a million inserts per second across the fan-out fleet, that is about a minute of the whole fleet's capacity, and the last followers see the post a minute late. With pull for celebrities, the cost moves to reads, so the celebrity's recent posts must be extremely hot in cache (replicated across cache nodes or held in-process) because every timeline read touches them. This is the classic hot key problem; the mitigation is replication of that key or a local cache with a short TTL.

## Deep dive 3: ranking
Moving from chronological to ranked changes the architecture into a pipeline:

```text
candidate generation  ->  feature hydration  ->  scoring  ->  filtering & mixing
 (in-network: timeline       (author affinity,     (ML model,   (diversity, dedup,
  cache, celebrity pulls;     post age, engagement,  light then   ads, policy)
  out-of-network: recs)       viewer history)        heavy)
```

- Candidates: a few hundred to a few thousand post ids from the precomputed timeline plus other sources (posts from similar users, trending).
- Features: counts, affinity between viewer and author, recency, media type. Fetched in bulk from feature stores.
- Scoring: a cheap model prunes to a few hundred, a heavier model scores the rest. Twitter's 2023 open-sourced recommendation code and its overview describe this shape: candidate sources, a light ranker, a heavy neural ranker, then heuristics and filters.
- Ranked feeds break simple cursor pagination because scores change; one solution is to rank a page set once per session and paginate over that snapshot.

## Deep dive 4: consistency and edge cases
- **Read-your-own-writes**: write the author's own timeline synchronously, or have the client insert its new post locally.
- **Deletes**: do not chase the id through millions of timelines; filter at hydration (the post cache returns "deleted") and let the id age out.
- **Unfollow**: filter at read time against the current follow set, or lazily rebuild.
- **New follow**: backfill a few recent posts of the newly followed account into the timeline asynchronously.
- **Cache loss**: a lost timeline shard is rebuilt from the posts store (pull) on next read. This is why the cache is a cache, not the source of truth.

## Failure modes
- Fan-out lag during spikes (big live events): the queue absorbs bursts; monitor consumer lag; degrade by temporarily pulling for more authors.
- Hot celebrity keys: replicate, local cache.
- Thundering herd on cold cache after a deploy: request coalescing so one rebuild per user.

## Common mistakes
- Picking pure push or pure pull and not noticing the skew problem.
- Storing full post objects in every timeline.
- Fanning out to all followers including dormant accounts.
- Forgetting the author's own post visibility.
- Talking about ranking only as "use ML" without the candidate / score / filter pipeline.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** the push/pull trade-off quantified, the celebrity fix, cache sizing, hydration and how ranking fits.

**60-second outline:** scope (post, follow, home timeline, chronological first); estimate (~15k reads/s, ~600 posts/s, ~120k fan-out inserts/s, timeline of 800 ids per active user); data model (time-sortable post ids, follows both directions, Redis lists of ids); hybrid fan-out with celebrity threshold and inactive-user skip; read path merges, hydrates and filters; ranking as candidate generation plus scoring.

**Follow-ups to expect:** "What is your celebrity threshold and how do you pick it?", "How do you handle a user who follows 5,000 accounts?", "How do you delete a post everywhere?", "What happens when the timeline cache cluster loses a node?", "How would you paginate a ranked feed?"
keyPoints: Fan-out on write precomputes each follower's timeline at post time: cheap reads, expensive writes for accounts with millions of followers.
Fan-out on read merges followees' recent posts at read time: cheap writes, expensive and slow reads for users who follow many accounts.
The standard answer is hybrid: push for normal accounts, pull for celebrities at read time, merged in the feed service.
Timelines cache only post ids (a few hundred per user); post bodies, authors and counts are hydrated from separate caches.
Ranking turns the feed into candidate generation, feature fetch and scoring; precomputed timelines become one candidate source among several.
interview: Design the home timeline for a Twitter-like service.
Fan-out on write or fan-out on read: how do you choose, and what do you do about celebrities?
How would you add ranking to a chronological feed?

check.q: A user with 50 million followers posts. Under pure fan-out on write, what is the main problem?
options: One post triggers 50 million timeline writes, delaying delivery and spiking load
check.why: Write amplification equals follower count. A celebrity post becomes tens of millions of cache inserts, which takes minutes and competes with all other fan-out work.

check.q: In a hybrid feed, what happens when a normal user opens their timeline?
options: The service reads only the precomputed timeline
The service reads the precomputed timeline and merges in recent posts from the celebrities they follow
The service queries every followee's posts
The client fetches each followee separately
check.why: Pushed posts from normal accounts are already in the cached timeline; posts from the few high-follower accounts are pulled at read time and merged by time or score.

check.q: Why do timeline caches usually store post ids rather than full post objects?
options: Full objects would be duplicated across millions of timelines and edits or deletes would have to update every copy
check.why: Storing ids keeps each timeline small (8 bytes per entry) and keeps one source of truth per post; hydration fetches bodies, author info and counts from shared caches.

lessons.title: Design a chat system (WhatsApp / Slack)
lessons.summary: Persistent connections and gateways, message storage partitioned by conversation, per-conversation ordering, delivery and read receipts, presence and group fan-out.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
A chat system moves small messages between users in near real time, stores them durably, and syncs them across every device a user owns. The hard parts are not the messages themselves; they are **connections** (millions of long-lived sockets), **routing** (which server holds the recipient's socket right now), **ordering and delivery guarantees** over unreliable mobile networks, **presence**, and **group fan-out**.

WhatsApp and Slack sit at two ends of the design space. WhatsApp is mostly 1:1 and small groups, phone-first, with end-to-end encryption and messages held on the server only until delivered (historically). Slack is channel-first: large channels, persistent searchable history, many integrations. Clarify which one the interviewer means.

## Requirements
**Functional**: 1:1 and group messaging (groups up to, say, 500 members; ask about larger channels), message history synced across devices, delivery and read receipts, online/last-seen presence, push notifications when offline, media attachments.
**Out of scope**: voice/video calls, end-to-end key management details, search (mention it as a separate index).

**Non-functional**: end-to-end latency under ~300 ms when both are online; no lost messages once the server acknowledged them; ordering correct within a conversation; high availability; mobile-friendly (battery, flaky networks).

## Estimation
Assume 500 million DAU, 40 messages sent per user per day, average message 200 bytes with metadata, 30% of DAU connected at peak.

```text
Messages:    5 x 10^8 x 40 = 2 x 10^10/day  -> 2 x 10^5 msg/s avg, ~5 x 10^5 peak
Deliveries:  group messages multiply this; assume avg 3 recipients -> ~1.5M deliveries/s peak
Storage:     2 x 10^10 x 200 B = 4 TB/day   -> ~1.5 PB/year if history kept forever
Connections: 1.5 x 10^8 concurrent sockets
             at ~100k-1M sockets per gateway (depends on runtime and memory)
             -> hundreds to low thousands of gateway servers
```

WhatsApp famously ran around 2 million connections per server on tuned FreeBSD/Erlang around 2012; on general-purpose stacks, plan for far fewer per box. The conclusions: connections are a first-class scaling dimension, storage is petabyte-class if history is retained, and writes are high enough that the message store must be partitioned and write-optimised.

## API
Mostly over the socket, with HTTP for history and uploads.

```text
WS  connect: wss://chat.example.com/ws  (auth token, device id, last_seq per conversation)

client -> server
  { type: "send", clientMsgId, conversationId, body, attachments[] }
  { type: "ack", conversationId, seq }               // delivered to this device
  { type: "read", conversationId, seq }              // read up to seq
  { type: "typing", conversationId }

server -> client
  { type: "sent", clientMsgId, conversationId, seq, ts }   // server accepted
  { type: "message", conversationId, seq, senderId, body, ts }
  { type: "receipt", conversationId, userId, kind: "delivered"|"read", upToSeq }
  { type: "presence", userId, status, lastSeen }

HTTP
  GET  /v1/conversations/{id}/messages?afterSeq=&limit=100
  POST /v1/uploads  -> presigned URL for media (goes straight to object storage)
```

## Data model

```text
conversations   conversation_id, type (direct|group), created_at
members         (conversation_id, user_id) + role, last_read_seq, muted
user_convs      (user_id, conversation_id, last_activity) -> inbox list
messages        PK (conversation_id, bucket), clustering seq DESC
                fields: seq, sender_id, client_msg_id, body, attachments, ts, edited, deleted
dedup           (sender_id, client_msg_id) -> seq   (TTL a few days)
```

Partitioning by conversation keeps a conversation's messages together for range reads ("give me everything after seq 4182"). A bucket (for example by time window) prevents one enormous partition for a very old, busy channel; Discord described exactly this pattern (channel id plus a time bucket) when explaining its Cassandra and later ScyllaDB message store. Wide-column stores fit because the dominant access is append and range-scan by key.

## High-level design

```text
 devices --- WSS ---> gateway servers (hold sockets, auth, heartbeats)
                         |     ^
             publish     |     |  deliver to socket
                         v     |
                 chat service (per-conversation owner)
                  | assigns seq, dedups, persists
                  v
            message store (wide-column, partitioned by conversation)
                  |
                  +--> fan-out: look up members -> session registry
                  |       (user_id -> [gateway, device] in Redis)
                  |       online  -> push to that gateway
                  |       offline -> notification service (APNs / FCM)
                  |
                  +--> event log (Kafka) -> search indexer, analytics

 presence service <-- heartbeats from gateways; TTL keys per user
```

**Send path**: the device sends `{clientMsgId, conversationId, body}` over its socket. The gateway forwards to the chat service instance that owns that conversation (by consistent hashing on conversation id, or a partition in a log). The owner checks dedup, assigns the next sequence number, persists, then acknowledges `sent` with the seq. Only after the durable write does the sender see one tick.

**Deliver path**: the owner looks up members and their sessions in the registry, pushes the message to each recipient's gateway, which writes it to the socket. The recipient's device acks; that becomes a `delivered` receipt routed back to the sender. Offline recipients get a push notification and fetch on reconnect.

Slack's write-up describes a similar shape: gateway servers hold websockets and subscribe to channels; channel servers, assigned by consistent hashing, own each channel's message flow.

## Deep dive 1: ordering
Global ordering across all chats is unnecessary and expensive. Users only perceive order within one conversation. So:
- Give each conversation a **single sequencer**: the chat-service owner for that conversation, or a single log partition keyed by conversation id. It assigns `seq = last + 1` atomically.
- Clients render by seq, not timestamp. Timestamps are for display only.
- Gaps are detectable: if a device has seq 10 and receives 12, it fetches 11 over HTTP.
- On owner failover, the new owner reads the last persisted seq before accepting writes. A lease or fencing token prevents two owners assigning the same seq during a split.

What about two people sending at the same moment? Whichever reaches the owner first gets the lower seq. Both devices then see the same order, which is the real requirement (consistency across participants, not "true" time).

## Deep dive 2: delivery guarantees and receipts
Networks drop. The protocol is at-least-once with idempotency:
1. Device generates `clientMsgId` (UUID) and stores the message locally as "pending".
2. Sends; retries with the same id until it receives `sent`.
3. Server dedups on `(sender, clientMsgId)`, returning the existing seq for duplicates.
4. Recipient devices ack seq; the server records per-device delivery and emits a receipt.

The familiar ticks map to state: one tick = server persisted; two ticks = delivered to at least one recipient device; blue/read = recipient read up to that seq. In groups, store `last_read_seq` per member rather than per-message rows: "read up to 4182" covers every earlier message and is one small update. A group's "read by" view is computed from members' `last_read_seq`.

Exactly-once delivery to the UI is achieved by dedup on the client too: the device ignores a seq it already has.

## Deep dive 3: connections and routing
- Gateways are stateful (they hold sockets) but contain no business logic. Keep them thin so they can be redeployed by draining connections gradually; clients reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter so a gateway restart does not cause a thundering herd.
- The **session registry** maps `user_id -> [(gateway_id, device_id)]`, stored in Redis with a TTL refreshed by heartbeats. Stale entries expire if a gateway dies.
- Heartbeats every 30-60 seconds keep NAT mappings alive and detect dead connections; mobile platforms limit background sockets, so offline delivery relies on APNs/FCM pushes.
- On reconnect, the client sends its last seq per active conversation; the server streams what is missing (or the client pages through HTTP for long gaps).

## Deep dive 4: group fan-out
For a 500-member group, one send becomes 500 deliveries. Options:
- **Fan-out on write to inboxes**: copy a pointer into each member's inbox. Simple reads; heavy for big groups.
- **Fan-out on delivery only**: store the message once per conversation, push to online members via the registry, and let offline members pull by seq on reconnect. This is what makes the conversation-partitioned store attractive.
- For huge channels (Slack channels with 100k members, Discord servers), gateways subscribe to channels they have members for, so the channel server publishes once per gateway rather than once per user. Discord has written about fanning out to very large guilds using Elixir processes per guild and relays.

## Deep dive 5: presence
Naively, every status change goes to every contact: N users times C contacts updates per change. Better:
- Gateways send heartbeats; the presence service stores `user_id -> online` with a TTL (say 60 seconds). Missing heartbeats mean offline without an explicit disconnect.
- Only push presence to users who are **actively viewing** a conversation list or chat with that person (subscribe on view, unsubscribe on leave).
- Debounce flapping (mobile networks drop for seconds); show "last seen" with coarse granularity.
- For very large groups, do not show live presence of every member; show a count.

## Storage, media and retention
Media goes directly to object storage via presigned URLs; messages hold references, and a CDN serves downloads. For end-to-end encrypted designs, the server stores ciphertext only and cannot search or moderate content, which changes features like search and multi-device sync (each device has its own keys; senders encrypt per device). Mention this trade-off if WhatsApp is the target.

## Failure modes
- Gateway crash: clients reconnect elsewhere; the registry TTL removes stale sessions; messages are already persisted so nothing is lost.
- Chat-service owner crash: ownership moves (consistent hashing or partition reassignment); the new owner reloads the last seq.
- Message store slow: back-pressure on sends; the sender keeps "pending" state and retries.

## Common mistakes
- Using timestamps for ordering.
- Acknowledging before the durable write.
- Promising exactly-once without dedup ids.
- Broadcasting presence to everyone.
- One giant partition per channel forever (no bucketing).
- Forgetting multi-device: receipts and sync are per device.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** connection management and routing, ordering, the receipt protocol, storage layout, presence cost, and group fan-out.

**60-second outline:** scope (1:1 and groups, receipts, presence, multi-device, offline push); estimate (~200k msgs/s, ~150M sockets, PB-scale history); WebSocket gateways plus session registry; per-conversation owner assigns seq after dedup and persists to a conversation-partitioned store; deliver via registry or push notification; receipts as last-delivered/last-read seq per member; presence via heartbeats with TTL, sent only to active viewers.

**Follow-ups to expect:** "How do you handle a 100k-member channel?", "What happens when a gateway dies mid-send?", "How does a new device get history?", "How would end-to-end encryption change this?", "How do you edit or delete a message?" (an edit is a new event referencing the original seq).
keyPoints: Clients hold a long-lived WebSocket to a gateway; a session registry maps user to gateway so any service can route a message to the right connection.
Ordering is only meaningful per conversation: assign a monotonically increasing sequence number per conversation at a single owner (a partition or channel server).
Delivery is at-least-once with client-generated message ids for dedup; receipts are just more messages flowing back (sent, delivered, read).
Store messages partitioned by conversation id and clustered by sequence; offline devices sync by asking for everything after their last seen sequence.
Presence is expensive at scale: use heartbeats with TTLs and fan presence out only to users who are currently looking.
interview: Design a chat system like WhatsApp or Slack.
How do you guarantee message ordering and delivery receipts in a chat system?
How do you implement online presence for millions of users?

check.q: Why is a per-conversation sequence number preferred over client timestamps for ordering?
options: Client clocks drift and can be wrong, and two messages can share a millisecond; a single sequencer gives a total order within the conversation
Timestamps are too large to store
check.why: Clocks on phones are unreliable and concurrent sends are common. A single owner per conversation (a partition leader or channel server) assigns seq 1, 2, 3, which every device can sort and detect gaps with.

check.q: A phone loses connection right after sending and retries the same message. How does the server avoid storing it twice?
options: The server delays all messages by 5 seconds
The client attaches a unique client message id and the server dedups on (sender, client id)
check.why: Retries make delivery at-least-once. A client-generated idempotency id lets the server return the original sequence number instead of inserting a duplicate.

check.q: What is the main cost driver of naive presence in a large system?
options: Broadcasting every online/offline change to every contact, including those who are not looking
check.why: Presence changes constantly; pushing each change to all contacts multiplies into enormous fan-out. Sending presence only to active viewers, batching and using TTL heartbeats cut it dramatically.

lessons.title: Design a ride-hailing service (Uber / Lyft)
lessons.summary: High-frequency driver location updates, geospatial indexing with geohash, quadtrees and H3, nearby search, dispatch and matching, and the trip state machine.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
A ride-hailing system continuously tracks where available drivers are, and when a rider requests a trip, finds good candidate drivers nearby, offers the trip, and manages the trip until payment. The defining problems are a **very high rate of location writes**, **fast spatial queries** over moving points, and **matching** that is correct (no driver assigned twice) and good (low pickup time, high acceptance).

The interviewer wants to see you separate the ephemeral, eventually consistent world (locations, ETAs) from the strongly consistent world (trip assignment, payments), and that you know at least one geospatial indexing technique in depth.

## Requirements
**Functional**: drivers go online and stream location; riders see nearby cars and an ETA; rider requests a ride; the system offers it to a driver who accepts or declines; live tracking during pickup and trip; fare calculation and payment at the end.
**Out of scope**: pooling, scheduled rides, surge pricing details (mention them as extensions), driver onboarding.

**Non-functional**: match within a few seconds; location freshness within ~5 seconds; never assign one driver to two trips; high availability per city; tolerate a city-level spike (concerts, rain).

## Estimation
Assume 5 million drivers online at global peak, location update every 4 seconds, 20 million trips a day.

```text
Location writes: 5 x 10^6 / 4 s        = 1.25 x 10^6 updates/s at peak
Update size:     ~100 B (driver id, lat, lng, heading, speed, ts, status)
Ingest bandwidth: 1.25 x 10^6 x 100 B   = ~125 MB/s
Live index memory: 5 x 10^6 drivers x ~200 B = ~1 GB  -> fits in memory, partition by city/region for locality
Trip requests:   2 x 10^7 / 10^5 s      = 200 req/s avg; peaks in one city can be far higher
Location history: 1.25 x 10^6 x 100 B x 10^5 s = ~12 TB/day if every point is kept
                  -> cold storage, sampled or compressed
```

Conclusion: the live index is small but must absorb more than a million writes per second; keep it in memory, partitioned geographically, and write history asynchronously to cheap storage. Requests are comparatively few, so matching can afford more computation per request.

## API

```text
Driver app
  WS / gRPC stream: { lat, lng, heading, speed, ts, status }   every ~4 s
  POST /v1/drivers/me/status  { status: "online"|"offline" }
  receives: { type: "offer", tripId, pickup, expiresAt }
  POST /v1/offers/{tripId}/accept | /decline

Rider app
  GET  /v1/nearby?lat=&lng=          -> { drivers: [{ lat, lng, heading }], etaSeconds }
  POST /v1/trips  { pickup, dropoff, product }  Idempotency-Key  -> { tripId, status: "matching" }
  WS   trip updates: { status, driverLocation, eta }
```

## Data model

```text
live driver index (in memory, per region)
  cell_id -> set of driver_ids
  driver_id -> { lat, lng, cell_id, status, ts, vehicle }

drivers (durable)   driver_id, vehicle, rating, city
trips (durable, strongly consistent)
  trip_id, rider_id, driver_id, status, pickup, dropoff, requested_at, fare, version
driver_state (strongly consistent)
  driver_id -> available | offered(trip_id, expires) | on_trip(trip_id) , version
location_history (append-only, object storage / time-series), partitioned by trip and day
```

## Geospatial indexing: the main deep dive
A naive `SELECT ... WHERE distance(lat, lng, ?) < 2 km` scans every row. Spatial indexes map 2D points to keys so "nearby" becomes a few key lookups.

### Geohash
Geohash interleaves the bits of longitude and latitude and encodes them in base32. Each extra character subdivides the cell, so a longer shared prefix means a smaller shared cell.

```text
precision  approx cell size
   4       ~39 km x 20 km
   5       ~4.9 km x 4.9 km
   6       ~1.2 km x 0.61 km
   7       ~153 m x 153 m
```

Nearby search: compute the rider's geohash at a precision whose cell is about the search radius (say 6), look up drivers in that cell **and its 8 neighbours**, then compute real distances and sort. Edge cases:
- **Boundary problem**: two points a metre apart can straddle a cell edge and share no prefix (worst case at the equator or the prime meridian, where even the first character differs). Always search neighbours.
- **Non-uniform cells**: cells are defined in degrees, so they shrink east-west towards the poles.
- **Density varies**: a 1 km cell in Manhattan can hold hundreds of drivers, in rural areas zero. Expand the search ring until you have enough candidates.

Redis implements this pattern for you: `GEOADD` stores members in a sorted set with a 52-bit geohash score, and `GEOSEARCH ... BYRADIUS 2 km ASC COUNT 20` returns nearby members. A sharded Redis keyed by city is a reasonable interview answer for the live index.

### Quadtrees
A quadtree recursively splits a region into four children until each leaf holds at most K points. It adapts to density: Manhattan becomes deep, deserts stay shallow. Search walks down to the rider's leaf and checks neighbouring leaves. The downside for moving drivers is churn: a million updates per second means constant removal and insertion, and splits/merges. It works best in memory per region, rebuilt or updated in place, and was a common answer in older Uber-style write-ups.

### H3 and S2
Uber built **H3**, a hexagonal hierarchical index: the globe is divided into hexagons at 16 resolutions (0 to 15), each cell has a 64-bit id, and every hexagon's six neighbours are equidistant from it. That makes "k-ring" searches (all cells within k steps) uniform, which matters for surge pricing and demand forecasting where you smooth values across neighbouring cells. At resolution 9 a cell averages roughly 0.1 square kilometres. To tile a sphere, every resolution contains exactly 12 pentagons, placed over oceans. Google's **S2** uses a cube projected onto the sphere with a Hilbert curve, giving square-ish cells and good locality for range scans.

| Technique | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|
| Geohash | Simple, string prefix, Redis support | Edge effects, distortion |
| Quadtree | Adapts to density | Updates churn, custom structure |
| H3 | Uniform neighbours, hierarchy, analytics | Not exact parent/child containment |
| S2 | Precise containment, Hilbert locality | Square cells, more complex API |

A good answer: "I'd key the live index by H3 resolution 8 or 9 cells (or geohash 6). Driver updates move the driver between cell sets when they cross a boundary. A nearby search queries the rider's cell plus a k-ring of neighbours, expanding until we have enough candidates."

```python
import h3

def candidate_cells(lat: float, lng: float, k: int = 1, res: int = 9) -> set[str]:
    origin = h3.latlng_to_cell(lat, lng, res)
    return set(h3.grid_disk(origin, k))   # origin plus all cells within k steps

def on_location(driver_id: str, lat: float, lng: float, index, drivers) -> None:
    cell = h3.latlng_to_cell(lat, lng, 9)
    prev = drivers.get(driver_id)
    if prev and prev["cell"] != cell:
        index[prev["cell"]].discard(driver_id)
    index.setdefault(cell, set()).add(driver_id)
    drivers[driver_id] = {"lat": lat, "lng": lng, "cell": cell}
```

(These are the H3 v4 Python function names.)

## High-level design

```text
 driver apps --stream--> location gateway --> location service (partitioned by region/cell)
                                                 |  updates in-memory index
                                                 |  publishes to Kafka (history, ETA models, surge)
                                                 v
                                          live geo index (Redis GEO / in-memory H3 maps)
 rider app --> API gateway --> trip service ----> dispatch / matching service
                                  |                 | 1. candidates from geo index
                                  |                 | 2. ETA via routing service (road graph)
                                  |                 | 3. rank, CAS driver_state, send offer
                                  v                 v
                            trips DB (strong)   driver_state store (strong, CAS)
                                  |
                       payments, notifications, trip tracking (WS)
```

## Deep dive: matching
1. **Candidates**: drivers in nearby cells who are available and match the product (car type).
2. **Rank by ETA, not straight-line distance**: a driver 300 m away across a river can be 10 minutes out. A routing service computes ETAs on the road graph (with traffic); this is the expensive step, so prune to the top 10-20 by distance first.
3. **Offer**: atomically move the chosen driver from `available` to `offered(trip, expires=now+15s)` with a compare-and-set on a version number. If the CAS fails, someone else got them; try the next candidate.
4. **Accept / timeout**: on accept, transition trip to `driver_assigned` and driver to `on_trip`. On decline or timeout, release the driver and offer to the next candidate.
5. **Batching** (a senior-level extension): instead of greedy first-come matching, collect requests over a short window (a second or two) in a region and solve an assignment problem that minimises total pickup time. This beats greedy when demand is dense.

Ownership per region avoids most contention: route all matching for an area to one dispatcher partition, so double assignment can only happen at region borders, which the CAS covers.

## The trip state machine

```text
requested -> matching -> driver_assigned -> driver_arrived -> in_progress -> completed -> paid
     \            \               \
      cancelled    no_drivers      cancelled (fee rules)
```

Store state transitions with a version and only allow valid transitions (conditional update `WHERE status = 'matching' AND version = 7`). Every transition emits an event for notifications, pricing and analytics.

## Reliability and scale
- **Partition by geography**: cities are natural shards. A busy city may need sub-partitions by cell.
- **Location service failure**: the index is rebuildable within seconds from the next round of updates (every driver sends again in ~4 s). That is why it can live in memory without heavy durability.
- **Trip data cannot be lost**: replicated database, idempotent trip creation (a rider tapping twice must not create two trips).
- **Spikes**: queue requests per region, show realistic ETAs, and use surge pricing to balance supply and demand.

## Common mistakes
- Querying a relational table with distance math per request.
- Ignoring cell boundaries.
- Using straight-line distance as the final ranking.
- Persisting every location update synchronously to a durable database.
- No atomic driver assignment, so two riders get the same car.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** whether you size the location write rate, pick and explain a spatial index, handle boundaries and density, separate eventually consistent location data from strongly consistent assignment, and design matching beyond "nearest".

**60-second outline:** scope; estimate ~1.25M location updates/s and a ~1 GB live index; in-memory geo index (Redis GEO or H3 maps) partitioned by city; nearby search = cell + neighbours, expand ring, rank by road ETA; offer via CAS on driver state with expiry; trip state machine in a strongly consistent store; history and analytics through Kafka.

**Follow-ups to expect:** "Why hexagons?", "How do you handle a driver crossing a partition boundary?", "How would you add pooling?", "How do you compute ETA cheaply?", "What happens if the dispatcher crashes after sending an offer?" (the offer has an expiry; state recovers from the driver_state store).
keyPoints: Driver locations are a write-heavy, ephemeral stream (an update every few seconds per driver); keep the live index in memory, persist history asynchronously.
Geohash turns lat/lng into a prefix-searchable string; neighbours across cell edges must be searched too, and cells distort near the poles.
H3 hexagons give uniform neighbour distance and a hierarchy of resolutions; Uber built it for surge pricing and supply/demand analysis.
Matching is more than nearest driver: ETA on the road graph, driver acceptance, batching requests over a short window and avoiding double assignment.
Trips are a state machine with strong consistency on assignment; location and ETA can be eventually consistent.

How would you index millions of moving driver locations for nearby search?
What is a geohash and what are its edge cases?

check.q: Why is searching only the rider's own geohash cell not enough to find nearby drivers?
options: A driver just across a cell boundary can be metres away but have a different prefix, so the 8 neighbouring cells must be searched too
check.why: Prefix sharing implies proximity, but proximity does not imply prefix sharing. Standard practice is to query the cell plus its 8 neighbours at a suitable precision, then filter by real distance.

check.q: What is a key advantage of H3 hexagons over square grid cells for ride-hailing analytics?
options: Hexagons can be stored as integers but squares cannot
Hexagons perfectly tile the sphere at every resolution with no exceptions
Hexagons are always exactly 1 km across
All six neighbours of a hexagon are the same distance from its centre, which makes ring searches and smoothing more uniform
check.why: Squares have edge and corner neighbours at different distances. Hexagons have one kind of neighbour, which simplifies k-ring searches and gradients. (H3 needs 12 pentagons per resolution to tile the sphere.)

check.q: Two dispatchers try to assign the same driver to different riders at the same time. What prevents a double assignment?
options: Eventual consistency in the location index
A conditional write on the driver's state (available -> offered) such as a compare-and-set or a lock with a lease
Sending both offers to the driver
Client-side checks in the rider app
check.why: The location index can be stale, but the assignment must be atomic. A CAS on the driver record or a per-driver owner process ensures only one offer wins.
