lessons.title: Design a video streaming platform (YouTube / Netflix)
lessons.summary: Resumable uploads, a DAG-based transcoding pipeline, HLS/DASH adaptive bitrate streaming, CDN and edge caching, and metadata and view counts at scale.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
A video platform has two very different halves. The **upload and processing** half takes a large raw file, makes it durable, and turns it into many encoded versions (resolutions, bitrates, codecs) cut into small segments. The **playback** half serves those segments to millions of players worldwide, letting each player adapt quality to its network in real time. Almost all the cost is in two places: compute for transcoding and bandwidth for delivery.

Clarify which product you are designing. **YouTube** ingests a huge volume of user uploads (YouTube has publicly cited more than 500 hours of video uploaded every minute), most of which are watched rarely: a long-tail problem. **Netflix** has a curated catalogue in the tens of thousands of titles, encoded very carefully once and pre-positioned in caches inside ISPs before people press play.

## Requirements
**Functional**: upload a video with title and description; process it into streamable formats; watch with adaptive quality on web, mobile and TV; search and browse; view counts, likes, comments; resume playback position.
**Out of scope**: live streaming (mention how it differs), monetisation, recommendations internals (treat as a service).

**Non-functional**: playback start under ~2 seconds; minimal rebuffering; uploads resumable over flaky networks; a published video should be watchable within minutes of upload; durable storage of originals; global reach.

## Estimation
YouTube-like assumptions: 500 hours uploaded per minute; 1 billion hours watched per day (a figure YouTube published years ago; treat as order of magnitude).

```text
Upload volume:  500 h/min x 60 x 24       = 720,000 hours/day
Raw size:       ~1 GB per hour at a typical upload bitrate (varies a lot)
                -> ~720 TB/day of originals
Encoded output: ladder of ~6 renditions x 2 codecs, total often ~1-2x original
                -> ~1 PB/day of new storage, before replication
Transcode compute: encoding is far slower than real time per CPU core for modern codecs;
                -> hundreds of thousands of cores (or hardware encoders) running continuously

Playback:       10^9 hours/day x 3,600 s / 10^5 s ~ 4 x 10^7 concurrent streams on average
                at ~3 Mbps average -> ~1.2 x 10^14 bit/s ~ 120 Tbps of egress
```

You do not need exact numbers, but the conclusion is unavoidable: egress at this scale cannot come from a few data centres. It must come from a CDN or from caches inside ISPs, and the encoding pipeline must be massively parallel.

## API

```text
POST /v1/videos                       { title, description, visibility }
   -> { videoId, uploadUrl (resumable session) }
PUT  <uploadUrl>  Content-Range: bytes 0-8388607/2147483648   (chunked, resumable)
POST /v1/videos/{id}/complete
GET  /v1/videos/{id}                  -> metadata, status (processing|ready), manifestUrl
GET  <cdn>/v/{id}/master.m3u8         -> HLS master playlist (or DASH .mpd)
GET  <cdn>/v/{id}/720p/seg_00042.m4s  -> media segment
POST /v1/videos/{id}/views            { positionSec, watchedMs } (batched)
```

## Data model

```text
videos       video_id, owner_id, title, description, status, duration, created_at, visibility
renditions   (video_id, rendition_id) -> codec, resolution, bitrate, manifest path, status
originals    object storage: originals/{video_id}/source.mp4  (cold tier after processing)
segments     object storage: v/{video_id}/{rendition}/seg_N.m4s + playlists
view_counts  video_id -> approximate counter (sharded counters + periodic rollup)
watch_state  (user_id, video_id) -> position, updated_at
```

Metadata is small and relational-friendly (sharded MySQL is what YouTube famously scaled with, via Vitess). Video bytes live only in object storage and caches.

## High-level design

```text
 creator --resumable upload--> object storage (originals)
    |                                  |
    +-- API: create/complete --> upload service --> "upload_complete" event
                                                          |
                                                 workflow orchestrator (DAG)
                         +----------------+---------------+--------------+
                         v                v               v              v
                     inspect/validate   split into     thumbnails     audio
                     (codec, length,    chunks (GOP-   + previews     transcode
                      safety scan)      aligned)
                                          |
                          parallel encode: chunk x rendition x codec  (worker fleet)
                                          |
                          stitch / package -> HLS + DASH (CMAF segments, manifests)
                                          |
                          publish: segments to origin storage, status=ready, notify

 viewer --> CDN edge --> (miss) --> regional shield --> origin storage
   |
   +--> API: metadata, manifest URL, signed tokens, watch state, view events --> Kafka --> counters
```

## Deep dive 1: the upload path
- **Resumable chunked uploads**: the client uploads 8-16 MB chunks to a session URL (the pattern used by Google's resumable upload protocol, tus, and S3 multipart). If the connection drops, it asks which bytes the server has and continues. Without this, a 4 GB upload on mobile rarely completes.
- **Direct to storage**: the API issues a presigned URL; bytes never pass through application servers.
- **Completion event**: when the last part is committed, emit `upload_complete` to start processing. Make the handler idempotent; storage notifications can be delivered more than once.

## Deep dive 2: the transcoding pipeline
Encoding a two-hour film sequentially into ten renditions on one machine would take many hours. The trick is parallelism along three axes:
1. **Split in time**: cut the source into chunks at keyframe (GOP) boundaries, for example 10-60 seconds each.
2. **Encode in parallel**: each chunk is encoded for each rendition and codec independently. A 2-hour video with 120 one-minute chunks and 12 rendition/codec pairs is 1,440 independent tasks.
3. **Reassemble and package**: concatenate encoded chunks, cut into delivery segments (2-6 seconds), and write HLS/DASH manifests. CMAF lets one set of fMP4 segments serve both HLS and DASH.

The orchestration is a **DAG** with retries per task, implemented with a workflow engine (Temporal, AWS Step Functions, or in-house systems like Netflix's Cosmos). Tasks must be idempotent and write outputs to deterministic paths so a retried task overwrites rather than duplicates.

**The bitrate ladder**: a typical H.264 ladder might run from about 240p at a few hundred kbps up to 1080p at roughly 4-6 Mbps, with 4K far higher; newer codecs (HEVC, VP9, AV1) reach similar quality at lower bitrates but cost much more compute to encode. Netflix's per-title encoding post (2015) showed that a fixed ladder wastes bits on simple content and starves complex content, so they compute a ladder per title from quality measurements; later work moved to per-shot optimisation. YouTube-scale platforms take a cheaper path for the long tail: encode fast, low-cost renditions first so the video is watchable within minutes, and add expensive codecs (AV1) only for videos that become popular.

**Prioritisation**: a creator with millions of subscribers gets priority; a backlog of rarely viewed uploads can wait for spare capacity.

## Deep dive 3: adaptive bitrate (ABR) streaming
HLS (RFC 8216) and MPEG-DASH both work the same way:

```text
master.m3u8 (lists renditions)
  #EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=800000,RESOLUTION=640x360
  360p/index.m3u8
  #EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=2800000,RESOLUTION=1280x720
  720p/index.m3u8
  #EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=5000000,RESOLUTION=1920x1080
  1080p/index.m3u8

720p/index.m3u8 (media playlist)
  #EXT-X-TARGETDURATION:6
  #EXTINF:6.0,
  seg_00001.m4s
  #EXTINF:6.0,
  seg_00002.m4s
  ...
```

The player downloads the master playlist, picks a starting rendition (often conservative for a fast start), and fetches segments over plain HTTP. After each segment it measures throughput and checks buffer level, then chooses the rendition for the next segment. Throughput-based algorithms estimate bandwidth; buffer-based algorithms (such as BOLA, used in dash.js) pick quality from how full the buffer is, which avoids oscillation. In browsers this is implemented with Media Source Extensions: JavaScript (hls.js, dash.js, Shaka Player) appends segment bytes to a `SourceBuffer`; Safari can also play HLS natively.

Because segments are ordinary immutable HTTP objects with stable URLs, CDNs cache them perfectly. That is the real reason HTTP-based ABR won over older streaming protocols.

**Live streaming** differs: segments are produced in real time, playlists update continuously, and latency is driven by segment duration and buffer depth. Low-latency HLS and DASH use partial segments to get end-to-end latency down to a few seconds.

## Deep dive 4: delivery and CDN
- **Edge caching**: popular segments are cached at CDN points of presence close to viewers. Hit ratios for popular content are very high; the long tail misses.
- **Origin shield**: a regional mid-tier cache in front of origin so a miss storm from hundreds of edges becomes one origin fetch.
- **Pre-positioning**: Netflix's Open Connect places appliances inside ISP networks and fills them during off-peak hours with what is predicted to be watched, so the vast majority of Netflix traffic is served from inside the viewer's ISP.
- **Signed URLs or tokens** with short expiry for access control; DRM (Widevine, FairPlay, PlayReady) for premium content.
- **Cost**: egress is usually the largest bill; better codecs directly reduce it, which is why the expensive AV1 encode pays off for popular titles.

## Deep dive 5: views and metadata
View counts are a high-write counter: batch view events from players, stream through Kafka, aggregate in windows, and update sharded counters. Validate views (minimum watch time, bot filtering) before counting; YouTube's displayed counts lag for exactly this reason. Watch position is a per-user upsert, written every few seconds of playback and debounced.

## Failure modes
- A transcoding worker dies: the orchestrator retries that task only; idempotent outputs make it safe.
- A bad encoder release corrupts output: keep originals, so you can re-encode; canary new encoder versions on a fraction of uploads.
- CDN region outage: multi-CDN with DNS or client-side failover; players retry a segment from an alternate host listed in the manifest.

## Common mistakes
- Streaming bytes through API servers or storing video in a database.
- Encoding sequentially on one machine.
- Forgetting that ABR needs aligned segments across renditions.
- Treating the CDN as an afterthought when it is the dominant cost and latency factor.
- Using one design for YouTube and Netflix without noting the long-tail difference.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** the upload path, pipeline parallelism, how ABR actually works, CDN strategy and cost awareness.

**60-second outline:** clarify YouTube vs Netflix; estimate upload volume and egress (tens to hundreds of Tbps), concluding CDN is mandatory; resumable presigned uploads; DAG pipeline splitting by time, encoding chunk x rendition in parallel, packaging CMAF for HLS/DASH; player chooses bitrate per segment; CDN edge plus shield plus origin; metadata in a sharded relational store; view counts via a stream.

**Follow-ups to expect:** "How do you make a new upload watchable in under 5 minutes?", "How would you add live streaming?", "How do you choose the ladder?", "What happens on a CDN miss storm for a viral video?", "How do you keep costs down for videos nobody watches?" (cheap codecs only, cold storage tiers, lazy encoding).
keyPoints: Uploads go straight to object storage via resumable, chunked uploads; API servers never proxy video bytes.
Transcoding is a DAG of parallel jobs: split into chunks, encode each rung of the bitrate ladder per codec, package into HLS/DASH, then publish.
Adaptive bitrate works because video is cut into few-second segments at several qualities; the player picks the next segment's quality from measured throughput and buffer.
Egress dominates cost and latency, so the CDN (or ISP-embedded caches like Netflix Open Connect) serves almost all bytes; origin protects itself with a shield tier.
YouTube is long-tail user content with heavy upload volume; Netflix is a smaller catalogue that can be pre-positioned. Ask which one.
interview: Design a video streaming platform like YouTube or Netflix.
How does adaptive bitrate streaming work end to end?
How would you design the transcoding pipeline for 500 hours of uploads per minute?

check.q: Why is video split into short segments (often 2-6 seconds) for HLS and DASH?
options: To make files smaller in total
Because browsers cannot play files longer than 10 seconds
So the player can switch quality at segment boundaries and CDNs can cache ordinary HTTP objects
check.why: Each segment is a cacheable HTTP object, and every rendition is cut at aligned boundaries, so the player can choose a different bitrate for the next segment without a gap.

check.q: What does Netflix's per-title encoding change compared with a fixed bitrate ladder?
options: It chooses the bitrate/resolution ladder per title based on its complexity, so simple content uses fewer bits for the same quality
It encodes every title at one bitrate
It removes the need for a CDN
check.why: An animated show needs far fewer bits than a grainy action film for the same perceived quality. Per-title (and later per-shot) optimisation picks ladders from measured quality curves.

check.q: Where should a new upload's bytes go first?
options: Through the API servers into the database
Into Kafka as one large message
Directly from the client to object storage using a presigned, resumable multipart upload
check.why: Presigned resumable uploads keep multi-gigabyte files off the API tier, survive flaky connections by resuming at the last chunk, and land the bytes where the transcoders read them.

lessons.title: Design a payment system (Stripe-like)
lessons.summary: Idempotency keys, payment state machines, double-entry ledgers, talking to card networks and PSPs, reconciliation, and why exactly-once is an illusion built from retries plus dedup.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
A payment system accepts a request to move money ("charge this card 49.00 EUR for order 812"), talks to external networks that are slow and sometimes ambiguous, and records exactly what happened so that money is never created, lost or moved twice. Throughput is modest compared with a social feed; **correctness under failure** is everything. The interviewer is testing whether you understand idempotency, state machines, ledgers, unreliable third parties and reconciliation.

A useful framing to say out loud: "In payments, every network call can fail in three ways: it succeeded, it failed, or we don't know. The design is mostly about the third case."

## Requirements
**Functional**: create a payment (authorise and capture a card, or other methods), refunds (full and partial), payouts to merchants, payment status queries, webhooks to merchants on status changes, balances per merchant.
**Out of scope**: fraud models (mention as a service on the path), card vaulting details (PCI scope, tokenisation), currency conversion.

**Non-functional**: no double charges, no lost payments; strong consistency for the ledger; auditable history (append-only); availability high but correctness wins over availability on the money path; latency of a few hundred ms to a few seconds is acceptable (card networks dominate).

## Estimation
Assume 10 million payments a day, peaking at 10x average during sales events.

```text
Payments:   10^7 / 10^5 s       = ~100/s average, ~1,000/s peak
Ledger:     each payment -> several transactions (auth, capture, fee, payout)
            x 2-4 entries each   -> ~5,000 entry writes/s peak
Storage:    10^7 payments x ~2 KB (payment + entries + events) = ~20 GB/day, ~7 TB/year
            retained for years (regulatory)
```

Conclusion: this volume fits comfortably in a well-run relational database cluster with serializable or carefully designed transactions, sharded by merchant if needed. You do not need exotic stores. Say so; reaching for eventual consistency here is a red flag.

## API

```text
POST /v1/payments
  Idempotency-Key: 7f1c...   (client-generated, unique per logical operation)
  { amount: 4900, currency: "eur", paymentMethod: "pm_...", merchantOrderId, capture: "automatic" }
  -> 201 { id: "pay_...", status: "requires_action" | "processing" | "succeeded" | "failed" }

POST /v1/payments/{id}/capture     Idempotency-Key
POST /v1/refunds                   Idempotency-Key  { paymentId, amount }
GET  /v1/payments/{id}
Webhooks -> merchant: { type: "payment.succeeded", data: {...} }  (signed, retried, at-least-once)
```

Amounts are integers in the smallest currency unit (cents). Never floats.

## Data model

```text
idempotency_keys  (merchant_id, key) PK, request_hash, status (in_progress|done),
                  response_code, response_body, locked_until, created_at  (expire after ~24h+)
payments          payment_id, merchant_id, amount, currency, status, psp_reference,
                  version, created_at, updated_at
payment_events    payment_id, seq, from_status, to_status, reason, ts   (append-only history)
ledger_accounts   account_id, owner (merchant | platform | customer_funds | psp_receivable), currency
ledger_txns       txn_id, payment_id, kind, created_at
ledger_entries    entry_id, txn_id, account_id, direction (debit|credit), amount
                  invariant: per txn, sum(debits) = sum(credits)
outbox            event_id, payload, published_at  (for webhooks and downstream consumers)
```

## High-level design

```text
 merchant server --> API gateway (auth, rate limit) --> payment service
                                                         |  1. idempotency check (key table)
                                                         |  2. create payment (state: created)
                                                         |  3. fraud/risk check
                                                         v
                                                  PSP / acquirer adapter  ---> card networks
                                                         |   (timeouts, retries with same ref)
                                                         v
                                   state transition + ledger entries + outbox  (one DB transaction)
                                                         |
                                     outbox relay --> Kafka --> webhook service --> merchant
                                                         \--> analytics, notifications

 nightly: settlement files from PSPs/banks --> reconciliation service --> diff report, alerts
 PSP webhooks --> webhook ingest (verify signature, dedup) --> payment service
```

## Deep dive 1: idempotency keys
Clients retry: networks time out, mobile apps resubmit, merchants' job runners rerun. Without protection, a retry is a second charge. Stripe's approach, described in its 2017 engineering post and API docs: the client sends an `Idempotency-Key` header; the server saves the result of the first request for that key, and any later request with the same key returns the saved result, including errors. Keys can be removed once they are at least 24 hours old, and reusing a key with different parameters is an error.

Implementation sketch in a relational database:

```sql
-- 1. claim the key atomically
INSERT INTO idempotency_keys (merchant_id, key, request_hash, status, locked_until)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3, 'in_progress', now() + interval '30 seconds')
ON CONFLICT (merchant_id, key) DO NOTHING
RETURNING *;
```

```ts
async function handleCreatePayment(req: Req): Promise<Res> {
  const claimed = await claimKey(req.merchantId, req.key, hash(req.body));
  if (!claimed) {
    const existing = await getKey(req.merchantId, req.key);
    if (existing.requestHash !== hash(req.body)) return conflict("key reused with different params");
    if (existing.status === "done") return replay(existing);      // same status + body as first time
    return conflict("request in progress, retry later");          // 409; client backs off
  }
  const result = await createPaymentAndCharge(req);              // uses the key as PSP reference too
  await finishKey(req.merchantId, req.key, result);               // store response atomically
  return result;
}
```

Details that separate good answers:
- Store the key, the state change and the response in the **same transaction** where possible. Brandur Leach's write-up goes further, splitting a request into atomic phases with recovery points so a crash mid-request can resume rather than restart.
- Pass an idempotency reference **downstream** to the PSP too, so your own retries to them are safe.
- Scope keys per merchant (or per API key).
- Distinguish retryable errors (do not cache a 500 caused by your own crash before any side effect) from final ones.

## Deep dive 2: the payment state machine

```text
created -> requires_action (3DS) -> processing -> authorised -> captured -> settled
    \              \                    \            \             \
     failed        failed              unknown       voided        refunded / partially_refunded
                                          |
                                (resolve via status query or PSP webhook)
```

Transitions are conditional updates: `UPDATE payments SET status='captured', version=version+1 WHERE id=$1 AND status='authorised' AND version=$2`. If zero rows changed, someone else moved it; re-read and decide. Each transition writes a `payment_events` row and the matching ledger entries in the same transaction. This makes the history auditable and the current status a reliable cache of it.

## Deep dive 3: double-entry ledger
Why not just a `balance` column? Because a balance column can be wrong with no way to tell why. In double-entry bookkeeping every transaction consists of entries that debit some accounts and credit others by equal amounts, so the system always balances. Balances are derived by summing entries (cached as running balances, but recomputable).

```text
Customer pays 100.00 EUR, platform fee 3.00:
txn 1 (capture)     debit  psp_receivable          100.00
                    credit merchant_payable          97.00
                    credit platform_fee_revenue       3.00
txn 2 (settlement)  debit  bank_cash                100.00
                    credit psp_receivable           100.00
txn 3 (payout)      debit  merchant_payable          97.00
                    credit bank_cash                 97.00
```

Properties you get: entries are **immutable** (corrections are new reversing entries, never edits); `sum(debits) = sum(credits)` is checkable per transaction and globally; every cent has a source and destination; audits and regulators can replay history. Square's "Books" post describes building exactly this as an immutable service; Modern Treasury's accounting series is a friendly primer on debits and credits for engineers.

## Deep dive 4: unreliable processors and "exactly once"
You cannot get exactly-once delivery across a network: a message can be lost or a reply can be lost, and the sender cannot tell which. What you can build is **exactly-once effect**: at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing.

- **Outgoing calls to the PSP**: on timeout, mark the payment `unknown`, then query the PSP using your reference, or wait for its webhook. Only retry the charge if the PSP supports idempotent requests with the same reference.
- **Incoming PSP webhooks**: verify the signature, dedup by event id, and apply as conditional state transitions. Webhooks can arrive out of order (a "succeeded" before a "processing"); the state machine must ignore stale transitions.
- **Publishing events**: use the **transactional outbox**: write the event row in the same transaction as the state change; a relay publishes it to Kafka afterwards. Consumers dedup by event id. This avoids the dual-write bug where the DB commits but the publish fails (or vice versa).
- **Outgoing webhooks to merchants**: at-least-once with exponential backoff for days; merchants are told to dedup by event id.

## Deep dive 5: reconciliation
Even with all of the above, bugs, partial outages and processor errors happen. Daily (or more often), ingest settlement reports from each PSP and bank, and match them line by line against the ledger:
- Matched: amounts and references agree.
- Missing internally: the PSP charged something we have no record of (dangerous: refund or investigate).
- Missing externally: we think it succeeded, the PSP disagrees.
- Amount mismatch: fees or currency differences.

Every mismatch becomes a case for automated resolution rules or a human. Reconciliation is not optional; mention it unprompted.

## Scaling and reliability
- A relational database with strong transactions is the right core. Shard by merchant id when one cluster is not enough; a payment and its ledger entries for a merchant live on one shard so the transaction stays local. Platform-wide accounts (fees) can be aggregated asynchronously.
- Multi-region: keep each merchant's writes homed in one region (or use a consensus-replicated database such as Spanner or CockroachDB) rather than multi-master with conflicts. Money does not tolerate last-writer-wins.
- Card data: tokenise at the edge so most services never see card numbers, shrinking PCI scope.

## Common mistakes
- Floats for money.
- Retrying a timed-out charge without an idempotent reference.
- A mutable balance column as the source of truth.
- Publishing events outside the database transaction.
- Claiming exactly-once delivery from Kafka solves it end to end. Kafka's exactly-once semantics cover Kafka-to-Kafka processing, not your call to a card network.
- No reconciliation.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** idempotency implementation, the unknown-outcome case, state machine discipline, ledger design, outbox, reconciliation.

**60-second outline:** scope (charge, refund, payout, webhooks); modest QPS, so a strongly consistent relational core; idempotency keys stored with request hash and response; payment state machine with conditional transitions; double-entry immutable ledger written in the same transaction; PSP adapter treats timeouts as unknown and resolves them; outbox to Kafka for webhooks; daily reconciliation against settlement files.

**Follow-ups to expect:** "What if the process crashes after charging but before saving?", "How long do you keep idempotency keys?", "How do you handle partial refunds?", "How would you go multi-region?", "How do you compute a merchant's balance quickly?" (running balance per account updated in the same transaction, verified against entry sums).
keyPoints: Every mutating call takes an idempotency key; the server stores the key with the request hash and the final response, and replays it on retry.
Model a payment as an explicit state machine with conditional transitions; never infer state from scattered rows.
Money movement is recorded in an append-only double-entry ledger: every transaction has entries that sum to zero, balances are derived.
External processors are unreliable: timeouts mean unknown outcome, so query status or wait for webhooks rather than blindly retrying a charge.
Reconciliation compares your ledger with processor and bank settlement files daily; it is how you catch the bugs your guarantees missed.

check.q: A client sends a charge with idempotency key K, times out, and retries with key K but a different amount. What should the server do?
options: Ignore the key and process normally
Reject the retry because the parameters do not match the original request for that key
check.why: A key binds to one request. Stripe returns an error when a key is reused with different parameters; silently charging the new amount would defeat the safety the key exists for.

check.q: Your call to the card processor times out. What is the safest next step?
options: Mark the payment failed and tell the user to try again
Mark it as unknown/pending and resolve by querying the processor with the same idempotency reference or waiting for its webhook
Retry the charge immediately with a new request id
check.why: A timeout does not mean the charge failed; it may have succeeded. Retrying with a new id risks a double charge, and failing it risks charging without delivering. Resolve the unknown state.

check.q: In a double-entry ledger, a customer pays 100 USD for an order. Which set of entries is correct?
options: Update the merchant balance column to +100
Debit customer funds/receivable 100 and credit the merchant payable 100, so the transaction sums to zero
check.why: Each transaction has at least two entries whose debits and credits balance. Balances are sums of entries, so money cannot appear or vanish without a matching entry.

lessons.title: Design search typeahead (autocomplete)
lessons.summary: Serving top-k suggestions per prefix in tens of milliseconds: tries with precomputed top-k, inverted indexes with edge n-grams, ranking signals, offline aggregation and multi-layer caching.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
Typeahead suggests completions as the user types: "how to" becomes "how to tie a tie", "how to screenshot on mac". Each keystroke is a request, the answer must arrive before the next keystroke, and the suggestions should be the ones people most likely want. It is a read-heavy, latency-critical system whose real complexity lives in two places: the **data structure** serving prefixes quickly, and the **offline pipeline** that decides what to suggest.

Do not confuse it with full search. Typeahead returns a handful of short strings (queries, products, people) for a prefix; it does not rank documents for a full query.

## Requirements
**Functional**: given a prefix, return the top 5-10 suggestions; suggestions reflect popularity and update at least daily (faster for trending); optional personalisation (recent searches) and filters (locale, category); remove offensive or legally blocked terms.
**Out of scope**: the search results page itself, spelling correction beyond basic fuzziness.

**Non-functional**: p99 under ~50-100 ms end to end including network (under ~10 ms in the service); highly available (degrade to no suggestions, never break search); eventual freshness is fine.

## Estimation
Assume 500 million searches per day, average 20 characters typed per search, but with debouncing the client sends roughly 6 requests per search.

```text
Requests:  5 x 10^8 x 6 / 10^5 s   = 30,000 QPS avg, ~90,000 peak
Corpus:    top 100 million distinct queries worth suggesting (long tail cut off)
           avg 25 bytes -> 2.5 GB of raw strings
Trie size: prefix nodes plus top-10 lists of ids at each node; many GB, but it
           fits in memory per server or sharded across a few
Logs:      5 x 10^8 queries/day x ~100 B = 50 GB/day of query logs to aggregate
```

Conclusion: the serving index fits in memory on a modest number of machines; the hot set (short prefixes) is tiny and can be cached at the edge; the pipeline processes tens of GB a day, a routine batch job.

## API

```text
GET /v1/suggest?q=how%20to%20t&locale=en-GB&limit=8
  -> { "q": "how to t", "suggestions": [ { "text": "how to tie a tie", "type": "query" }, ... ] }
  Cache-Control: public, max-age=300   (for non-personalised responses)
```

Personalised entries (your recent searches) are merged client-side or by a separate small call, so the main response stays cacheable.

## Data model

```text
offline:
  query_log      (ts, query_normalised, locale, user_hash, clicked)
  query_stats    (query, locale) -> decayed_count, last_seen, ctr
serving:
  trie / FST per locale: prefix -> top-k [(suggestion_id, score)]
  suggestion table: id -> display text, type, metadata
  blocklist: normalised terms never shown
```

## High-level design

```text
 user types --debounce 100-150 ms--> browser cache --> CDN (short prefixes, non-personal)
                                                         |
                                                   suggest service (stateless, sharded index in memory)
                                                         |
                                     +-------------------+------------------+
                                     |                                      |
                             prefix index shards                     personalisation
                             (trie/FST, top-k per node)              (recent searches, per user)

 offline pipeline:
   search logs --> Kafka --> stream job (trending, last hour, decayed counts)
                     \--> batch job (daily: normalise, filter, aggregate, score)
                                  |
                            index builder -> immutable index snapshot -> object storage
                                  |
                            suggest servers download + hot-swap the snapshot
```

## Deep dive 1: the trie
A trie stores strings character by character; a node represents a prefix. Walking `h -> o -> w` reaches the node for "how". To answer quickly, each node stores the precomputed **top-k completions** of its subtree with scores. A lookup is O(length of prefix) plus returning k items, regardless of how many completions exist.

```ts
type Node = { children: Map<string, Node>; top: { id: number; score: number }[] };

function suggest(root: Node, prefix: string, k = 8): number[] {
  let node: Node | undefined = root;
  for (const ch of prefix) {
    node = node.children.get(ch);
    if (!node) return [];
  }
  return node.top.slice(0, k).map((s) => s.id);
}

// build time: after inserting all queries, fill top-k bottom-up
function fillTop(node: Node, k: number, terminal?: { id: number; score: number }): void {
  const candidates = terminal ? [terminal] : [];
  for (const child of node.children.values()) {
    fillTop(child, k);
    candidates.push(...child.top);
  }
  node.top = candidates.sort((a, b) => b.score - a.score).slice(0, k);
}
```

Engineering details:
- **Memory**: a naive pointer-per-character trie is huge. Compress chains (radix/Patricia tree), store suggestion ids not strings, or use a **finite state transducer** (FST). Andrew Gallant's post on FSTs shows how sharing prefixes and suffixes compresses large key sets dramatically; Lucene's completion suggester (used by Elasticsearch) is built on in-memory FSTs.
- **Updates**: never mutate the serving trie per query. Rebuild from aggregated stats in batch (hourly or daily), publish an immutable snapshot, and have servers swap it atomically. A small "trending" overlay built from streaming counts can be merged at query time for freshness.
- **Sharding**: by prefix range (a-f, g-m...) is uneven because some letters are far more common; shard by hash of the first two or three characters, or simply replicate the whole index if it fits, which is simpler and avoids fan-out.

## Deep dive 2: inverted index alternative
An inverted index maps tokens to the documents (here, suggestion strings) containing them. For typeahead, index each suggestion with **edge n-grams**: "iphone" becomes "i", "ip", "iph", "ipho", "iphon", "iphone". Typing "iph" is then an exact token lookup. Because every token of the phrase is indexed, "pro" matches "iphone pro max" (infix by word), which a plain trie cannot do.

| | Trie / FST with top-k | Inverted index (edge n-grams) |
|---|---|---|
| Latency | Lowest, predictable | Low, but scoring at query time |
| Matching | Prefix of whole string | Prefix of any word, filters, fuzzy |
| Memory | Compact with FST | Larger (n-gram expansion) |
| Ranking | Precomputed static scores | Dynamic scoring, boosts, filters |
| Updates | Rebuild snapshots | Near-real-time indexing |
| Example | Lucene completion suggester | Elasticsearch search_as_you_type |

Rule of thumb: query suggestions on a web search engine fit a trie/FST well (prefix of whole query, static popularity). Product or people search with filters, typo tolerance and token matching fit an inverted index. Many real systems use both: a fast prefix index for the top results and an n-gram index for the long tail.

## Deep dive 3: ranking
Scores are computed offline from query logs:
- **Popularity with time decay**: `score = sum over occurrences of exp(-age / tau)`, so last week counts more than last year.
- **Click-through**: a suggestion that people pick and then click results is better than one they ignore.
- **Freshness / trending**: a streaming job detects queries whose rate spikes relative to their baseline ("earthquake now") and boosts them for hours.
- **Context**: locale, language, device; personalisation from the user's own recent searches merged on top.
- **Policy filters**: remove offensive, dangerous or legally blocked completions before indexing and again at serving time with a blocklist that can be hot-updated. Suggestions are product speech; this is a real requirement at every major search company.

Normalise before counting: lowercase, Unicode normalisation (NFKC), collapse whitespace, strip punctuation as appropriate per language.

## Deep dive 4: caching and the client
- **Client**: debounce (around 100-150 ms), cancel in-flight requests when a new keystroke arrives (`AbortController`), cache responses per prefix in memory so backspace is instant, and ignore out-of-order responses.
- **CDN**: one- and two-character prefixes are a tiny set with enormous traffic. Cache non-personalised responses at the edge for minutes.
- **Service**: an LRU of recent prefixes in each server; hit rates are high because prefix popularity is skewed.

## Failure modes and operations
- Bad index snapshot (corrupted or a blocklist miss): keep the previous snapshot and roll back instantly; validate snapshots (size, sample queries, blocklist check) before publishing.
- Pipeline delay: suggestions get stale but still work; alert on snapshot age.
- Service overload: shed load by returning empty suggestions; search must still work.

## Common mistakes
- Updating the trie on every query in the serving path.
- Walking subtrees at query time instead of precomputing top-k.
- Forgetting debouncing and client caching.
- No content filtering.
- Sharding by first letter and creating hot shards.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** the data structure choice and its memory, how suggestions get updated, ranking signals, latency budget and caching layers.

**60-second outline:** scope (top-k per prefix, daily freshness plus trending, locale); ~30k QPS with debouncing; in-memory trie/FST with top-k per node, built offline from decayed query counts and published as immutable snapshots; trending overlay from a stream job; caching at client, CDN and service; inverted index with edge n-grams when infix, filters or fuzzy matching are needed; blocklist at build and serve time.

**Follow-ups to expect:** "How do you handle typos?" (fuzzy matching with edit distance on an FST or n-gram index), "How fast can a trending term appear?", "How would you personalise without breaking caching?", "How big is the trie, really?", "How do you support many languages?"
keyPoints: The latency budget is tight (suggestions must render while the user types), so serve from memory and precompute as much as possible.
A trie with the top-k completions stored at each node answers a prefix in O(prefix length); updates are batched offline, not per query.
An inverted index with edge n-grams or a completion suggester handles mid-word matches, typos and filters better, at higher memory and query cost.
Ranking blends popularity (time-decayed), freshness, personalisation and context; the data pipeline aggregates query logs in batch and streaming layers.
Caching works at every layer: browser, CDN for short prefixes, and in-service caches, because short prefixes are few and extremely hot.

check.q: Why store the top-k completions at every trie node instead of walking the subtree at query time?
options: Walking the subtree of a short prefix like 'a' can touch millions of nodes; precomputed top-k makes every lookup O(prefix length)
check.why: The cost moves from query time to build time. Memory grows (k entries per node), but query latency becomes predictable and tiny.

check.q: Which requirement most strongly pushes you from a pure prefix trie to an inverted index?
options: Matching words in the middle of a phrase (typing 'pro' should match 'iphone pro max') and filtering by category
check.why: A trie matches only from the start of the indexed string. Infix and token matches, filters and fuzzy matching are natural in an inverted index with n-gram analysis.

check.q: A typeahead service sees 50,000 requests per second. What is the cheapest large win on the client side?
options: Debounce keystrokes (for example 100-150 ms) and cache prior responses per prefix in the client
Send the full query log to the server
check.why: Most keystrokes happen in quick bursts. Debouncing cuts requests substantially, and a backspace or repeated prefix can be served from a local cache with no request at all.

lessons.title: Design a distributed rate limiter
lessons.summary: Token bucket, leaky bucket, fixed and sliding windows; atomic counters in Redis with Lua; where the limiter sits; failure behaviour; and limiting across regions without a global lock.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
A rate limiter caps how many requests a client (user, API key, IP, tenant) can make in a period, so one caller cannot exhaust shared capacity, abuse an endpoint, or run up costs. On one server it is a counter in memory. In a fleet of hundreds of servers behind a load balancer, the counter has to be shared, fast, and correct enough under concurrency, and the limiter must not become the outage itself.

Interviewers use this problem to test algorithms, atomicity in distributed state, latency budgets, failure behaviour and multi-region trade-offs, all in a small surface.

## Requirements
Clarify these, they change the design:
- **What is limited**: per user, per API key, per IP, per endpoint, per tenant, globally? Usually several layers.
- **Limits**: "100 requests per second with bursts to 200", "1,000 per day".
- **Accuracy**: is a 1-5% overshoot acceptable? For abuse protection, yes. For billing quotas, maybe not.
- **Where**: API gateway, service mesh sidecar, inside the service, or a client library.
- **Latency budget**: the limiter check should add about a millisecond, not tens.
- **Behaviour when over**: reject with 429, queue, or degrade?

Stripe's write-up is a good model of layering: a request rate limiter (per user, token bucket), a concurrent requests limiter, and load shedders that drop low-priority traffic when the fleet is overloaded.

## Estimation
Assume an API with 1 million requests per second at peak across 10 million API keys, one limiter check per request.

```text
Limiter ops:  10^6 checks/s -> one Redis round trip each
              a single Redis node handles on the order of 10^5 simple ops/s;
              -> a Redis Cluster with tens of shards, keyed by client id
Memory:       10^7 keys x ~100 B (key name + counters + TTL overhead) = ~1 GB
Latency:      same-AZ Redis round trip ~0.2-1 ms
```

Conclusion: memory is trivial, throughput needs sharding, and latency forces the counter store to live in the same region (ideally the same zone) as the API servers.

## The algorithms

### Fixed window counter
Key `rl:{client}:{minute}`, `INCR`, set `EXPIRE` on first increment, reject when count exceeds the limit. Simplest and cheapest. Flaw: bursts at boundaries. A client can send the full limit at the end of one window and again at the start of the next, briefly doubling the rate.

### Sliding window log
Store a timestamp per request in a sorted set; on each request remove entries older than the window, count, and add. Exact, but memory is O(requests in window) per client, which is expensive for high limits.

### Sliding window counter
Keep counts for the current and previous fixed windows and weight the previous one by how much of it still overlaps the sliding window:

```text
estimate = prev_count x (window - elapsed_in_current) / window + current_count
```

Cloudflare described using exactly this approximation for its rate limiting, noting that in their analysis of real traffic it was very close to exact. Two counters per client, smooth limits, cheap.

### Token bucket
A bucket holds up to `capacity` tokens and refills at `rate` per second. Each request takes a token; no token means rejected. Allows bursts up to capacity while enforcing the long-run rate. You do not need a timer: store `tokens` and `last_refill` and compute the refill lazily on each request. This is the most common default (Stripe, AWS API Gateway, many gateways).

### Leaky bucket
Requests enter a queue that drains at a fixed rate; overflow is dropped. Produces a perfectly smooth output rate, which suits protecting a downstream with fixed capacity, but adds queueing latency. As a meter (no queue), it is equivalent to a token bucket viewed from the other side. **GCRA** (generic cell rate algorithm) implements leaky-bucket semantics with a single stored timestamp per key ("theoretical arrival time"); Brandur's post explains it and it is what libraries like redis-cell use.

| Algorithm | Bursts | Memory per key | Accuracy | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fixed window | 2x at edges | 1 counter | Coarse | Simplest |
| Sliding log | None | O(requests) | Exact | Expensive |
| Sliding counter | Smooth | 2 counters | Approximate | Great default for windows |
| Token bucket | Up to capacity | 2 values | Exact for its model | Most common |
| Leaky bucket / GCRA | Smooth output | 1-2 values | Exact for its model | Shaping |

## API and headers
The limiter itself is usually an internal library or sidecar call: `allow(key, cost=1) -> { allowed, remaining, resetAt }`. Externally, return `429 Too Many Requests` (RFC 6585) with `Retry-After`, plus informational headers. Many APIs use `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining` and `X-RateLimit-Reset`; the IETF httpapi working group has a draft standardising `RateLimit` and `RateLimit-Policy` headers.

## High-level design

```text
 clients --> load balancer --> API gateway / sidecar (limiter check) --> services
                                     |    \
                                     |     local in-process limiter (fallback, coarse per-instance cap)
                                     v
                           Redis Cluster (counters, keyed by client; hash tags keep a client's keys on one shard)
                                     ^
                           rules service: limits per plan/tenant/endpoint, cached in gateways, hot reload
```

Rules live in configuration (per plan, per endpoint, per tenant overrides) pushed to gateways; the counter state lives in Redis.

## Deep dive 1: atomic token bucket in Redis
Two app servers doing `GET tokens` then `SET tokens-1` can both pass when one token remains. Use a Lua script so the read-modify-write is atomic and costs one round trip:

```text
-- KEYS[1] = bucket key; ARGV = capacity, refill_per_sec, now_ms, cost
local cap    = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local rate   = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local now    = tonumber(ARGV[3])
local cost   = tonumber(ARGV[4])
local b      = redis.call("HMGET", KEYS[1], "tokens", "ts")
local tokens = tonumber(b[1]) or cap
local ts     = tonumber(b[2]) or now
tokens = math.min(cap, tokens + (now - ts) / 1000 * rate)
local allowed = 0
if tokens >= cost then
  tokens = tokens - cost
  allowed = 1
end
redis.call("HSET", KEYS[1], "tokens", tokens, "ts", now)
redis.call("PEXPIRE", KEYS[1], math.ceil(cap / rate * 1000) + 1000)
return { allowed, tokens }
```

Notes: pass `now` from the app server or use Redis `TIME` inside the script (newer Redis versions replicate script effects, which makes `TIME` safe); clock skew between app servers slightly distorts refill, which is usually acceptable. The `PEXPIRE` makes idle buckets disappear, keeping memory bounded.

## Deep dive 2: performance and hot keys
- One Redis round trip per request is fine at ~1 ms. To cut it further, **batch locally**: each gateway instance takes a lease of N tokens from Redis and spends them locally, returning to Redis only when exhausted. This trades accuracy (up to N x instances overshoot) for throughput.
- A single abusive key can make one Redis shard hot. A local in-process limiter in front of Redis rejects obvious floods without touching Redis at all.
- Pipeline or use Redis Cluster hash tags so all keys for one client live on one shard and multi-key scripts work.

## Deep dive 3: failure behaviour
- **Redis down or slow**: set a tight timeout (a few ms). On failure, **fail open** for general API limits, applying a local per-instance limit as a safety net, and alert. Fail **closed** for limits that exist for security (login attempts, OTP verification), where letting traffic through is the bigger risk.
- **Retries amplify load**: clients that retry on 429 without backoff make overload worse. Return `Retry-After` and document exponential backoff with jitter. The Google SRE book's chapters on handling overload and cascading failures describe this dynamic.

## Deep dive 4: multi-region
A user's requests may hit several regions. A single global counter would add a cross-region round trip (tens to 100+ ms) to every request, which defeats the purpose. Options:
1. **Home region**: route each tenant's traffic or limiter checks to its home region. Accurate, but adds latency for traffic landing elsewhere.
2. **Split the quota**: give each region a share (static, or weighted by recent traffic). No cross-region calls; under-utilises when traffic is uneven.
3. **Local counting with async sync**: each region enforces locally against a global view that is gossiped or replicated every few hundred ms. Overshoot is bounded by `sync interval x rate x regions`. This is the common pragmatic answer.
4. **CRDT counters** (G-counters per region) give a mergeable global count with eventual convergence.

Say the trade-off plainly: exact global limits and low latency are incompatible; choose which one the product needs. Abuse protection tolerates brief overshoot; a hard monthly quota tied to billing can be reconciled afterwards.

## Where to put the limiter
- **Edge / CDN / WAF**: IP-based limits against floods, before traffic reaches you.
- **API gateway or sidecar** (Envoy global rate limiting calls an external rate limit service): per key, per route, consistent across services.
- **In the service**: business-aware limits (per tenant per expensive operation, "5 exports per hour").
- **Client-side**: SDKs that self-throttle to avoid 429s.
Most real systems layer two or three of these.

## Common mistakes
- Non-atomic read-modify-write against Redis.
- Fixed windows without acknowledging the boundary burst.
- Synchronous cross-region calls on every request.
- No decision on fail-open vs fail-closed.
- Forgetting `Retry-After` and headers, so clients cannot behave.
- Keys without TTLs, so memory grows forever.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** algorithm choice with trade-offs, atomic shared state, latency, failure behaviour and multi-region.

**60-second outline:** clarify keys, limits and accuracy; token bucket (or sliding window counter) per client; counters in a sharded Redis via an atomic Lua script, ~1 ms per check; rules from a config service; gateway or sidecar placement with a local fallback limiter; fail open except for security limits; 429 with Retry-After; multi-region via per-region quotas or local enforcement with async sync, accepting bounded overshoot.

**Follow-ups to expect:** "How do you limit concurrent requests, not rate?" (a counter incremented on start and decremented on finish, with a TTL to recover from crashes), "How do you rate limit by cost, such as LLM tokens?" (variable `cost` per request), "How would you test it?", "What overshoot do you get with local token leases?"
keyPoints: Token bucket allows controlled bursts and is the common default; sliding window counters approximate exact limits cheaply; fixed windows allow double bursts at boundaries.
In a fleet, counters must be shared: Redis with an atomic Lua script (or INCR plus EXPIRE) keyed by client and window is the standard design.
Decide fail-open vs fail-closed explicitly: most API limiters fail open when Redis is down, with a local in-process fallback limit.
Multi-region limits trade accuracy for latency: split the quota per region, or sync counts asynchronously and accept brief overshoot.
Return 429 with Retry-After and rate-limit headers so well-behaved clients back off instead of hammering.

check.q: With a fixed window of 100 requests per minute, how many requests can a client send in a short burst around a window boundary?
options: Up to about 200 (100 at 0:59 and 100 at 1:00)
check.why: Each window resets independently, so the end of one and the start of the next can both be fully used within a couple of seconds. Sliding windows and token buckets avoid this.

check.q: Why do Redis-based limiters often use a Lua script instead of separate GET and SET calls?
options: Redis cannot store integers without Lua
Lua scripts are replicated to all regions automatically
The script runs atomically on the Redis server, so concurrent requests cannot both read the old value and exceed the limit
check.why: Read-modify-write from many app servers races. Redis executes a script without interleaving other commands, giving an atomic check-and-update in one round trip.

check.q: Redis for the limiter becomes unreachable. For a public API's per-user limit, what is the usual choice?
options: Fail open with a conservative local per-instance limit, and alert
check.why: The limiter protects the service; taking the whole API down because the limiter is unhealthy is usually worse. A local fallback still caps abuse per instance. Security-sensitive limits (login attempts) may justify failing closed.

lessons.title: Design a notification system
lessons.summary: Multi-channel delivery (push, email, SMS, in-app) with priorities, user preferences, deduplication, rate limits and quiet hours, retries through unreliable providers, and tracking.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
A notification system takes events from many product services ("order shipped", "new message", "password changed", "weekly digest") and turns them into messages on the right channels: mobile push, email, SMS, in-app inbox, sometimes web push or chat apps. It sounds like plumbing, but it has real design problems: **priorities** (an OTP must arrive in seconds even during a campaign), **user preferences and policies**, **deduplication** across retries, **unreliable third-party providers**, **fan-out** to millions, and **tracking** delivery and engagement.

The cleanest way to present it is as a pipeline of independent stages connected by queues.

## Requirements
**Functional**: services send a notification request (user or segment, template, data, priority); deliver via push (APNs, FCM), email, SMS and in-app; per-user preferences per category and channel; quiet hours and frequency caps; templates with localisation; delivery status and open/click tracking; scheduled and bulk campaigns.
**Out of scope**: the campaign authoring UI, ML send-time optimisation (mention as extension).

**Non-functional**: transactional notifications delivered within seconds (p99 under ~5-10 s to the provider); bulk campaigns of tens of millions completed within hours without hurting transactional latency; no duplicates in normal operation; no lost transactional messages; respect legal requirements (unsubscribe for marketing email, consent for SMS).

## Estimation
Assume 100 million users; per day 300 million push, 50 million email, 5 million SMS; campaigns spike to 20 million sends in an hour.

```text
Steady push:   3 x 10^8 / 10^5 s       = ~3,000/s
Email:         5 x 10^7 / 10^5 s       = ~500/s
SMS:           5 x 10^6 / 10^5 s       = ~50/s  (most expensive per message by far)
Campaign peak: 2 x 10^7 / 3,600 s      = ~5,500/s extra on one channel
Records:       ~3.5 x 10^8 notifications/day x ~500 B log = ~175 GB/day of delivery logs
Device tokens: 10^8 users x ~2 devices = 2 x 10^8 tokens
```

Throughput is moderate; the challenge is isolation (campaign spikes vs transactional), provider limits, and cost control on SMS.

## API

```text
POST /v1/notifications
  Idempotency-Key: order-812-shipped
  {
    "userId": "u_123",                 // or "segmentId" for bulk
    "category": "order_updates",       // maps to preferences
    "priority": "high" | "normal" | "low",
    "template": "order_shipped",
    "data": { "orderId": "812", "eta": "2026-10-06" },
    "channels": ["push", "email"],     // optional; else policy decides
    "sendAt": null,                    // or a scheduled time
    "expiresAt": "..."                 // do not send after this (e.g. OTP)
  }
  -> 202 { "notificationId": "n_..." }

GET  /v1/notifications/{id}            -> per-channel status
GET  /v1/users/{id}/inbox?cursor=      -> in-app notifications
PUT  /v1/users/{id}/preferences        { category -> channels on/off, quietHours, timezone }
POST /v1/devices                       { userId, platform, token }
```

The 202 is deliberate: intake only validates and enqueues.

## Data model

```text
notifications   notification_id, idempotency_key UNIQUE, user_id, category, priority,
                template, data, created_at, expires_at
deliveries      (notification_id, channel) -> status (queued|sent|delivered|failed|suppressed),
                provider, provider_msg_id, attempts, last_error, timestamps
preferences     user_id -> { category: { push: bool, email: bool, sms: bool } }, quiet_hours, tz, locale
devices         device_id, user_id, platform, token, active, last_seen
templates       (template, channel, locale, version) -> subject/body with placeholders
inbox           (user_id, created_at DESC) -> notification summary, read flag
dedup           key -> 1 with TTL (Redis)
```

## High-level design

```text
 product services --> notification API (auth, validate, idempotency) --> intake queue (Kafka)
                                                                        |
                                           +----------------------------+
                                           v
                              policy & routing workers
                              - load preferences, consent, quiet hours (user tz)
                              - frequency caps / per-user rate limits
                              - choose channels, drop expired, dedup
                              - expand segments into per-user jobs (bulk)
                                           |
                                    render workers (templates, locale)
                                           |
              +-------------------+--------+---------+------------------+
              v                   v                  v                  v
        push queues          email queues       SMS queues          in-app writer
       (high|normal|low)    (high|normal|low)  (high|normal)        (inbox DB + live push
              |                   |                  |                via websocket/SSE)
        push workers         email workers      SMS workers
        APNs / FCM           SES / SendGrid     Twilio / others
              \                   |                  /
               +---- provider callbacks / webhooks --+--> status tracker --> deliveries DB, analytics
                                                       \--> device registry cleanup (invalid tokens)
 scheduler: delayed and scheduled sends (time-bucketed store polled each minute)
```

## Deep dive 1: priorities and isolation
- Separate topics or queues per channel and priority, each with its own worker pool and autoscaling. Transactional high-priority traffic gets reserved capacity.
- Bulk campaigns are throttled at the expansion step (for example, release 5,000 users per second into the queues) so they never flood downstream stages.
- Respect provider throughput limits per account; a token bucket per provider protects you from being throttled or flagged.
- `expiresAt` lets workers drop stale messages: an OTP that is five minutes late is useless, and a "your driver is here" push after the ride is harmful.

## Deep dive 2: deduplication
Duplicates come from three places: producers retrying the API call, queues redelivering after a worker crash, and providers or retries sending twice.
1. **API idempotency**: the `Idempotency-Key` (for example `order-812-shipped`) is unique in the notifications table; a retry returns the existing id.
2. **Worker-level dedup**: before sending, `SET dedup:{notificationId}:{channel} 1 NX EX 86400` in Redis. If the key exists, skip. Record the attempt in the deliveries table.
3. **Content-level collapse**: some events are noisy ("X liked your photo" 40 times). Aggregate within a window ("X and 39 others liked your photo") or use provider collapse keys (APNs `apns-collapse-id`, FCM collapse keys) so only the latest version is shown.

Be honest about the window: if a worker crashes after the provider accepted the message but before recording it, a retry can duplicate. That is why the effective guarantee is at-least-once with best-effort dedup; for most notifications this is acceptable, and for OTPs a duplicate is harmless while a loss is not.

## Deep dive 3: preferences and policy
Policy evaluation is a pure function worth writing as one: `(notification, preferences, user state, now) -> channels to send | suppressed(reason)`.
- **Category preferences**: users opt out per category and channel. Some categories are mandatory (security alerts, legal notices).
- **Quiet hours** in the user's own timezone: defer low-priority messages until the window ends; never defer critical ones.
- **Frequency caps**: at most N marketing pushes per day per user, implemented with the same counters as a rate limiter.
- **Channel fallback**: if push is disabled or no active device, fall back to email for important categories.
- **Legal**: marketing email must honour unsubscribe; SMS requires consent in many jurisdictions.
- Cache preferences close to the workers (they are read on every message, written rarely) and invalidate on update.

## Deep dive 4: providers, retries and failure
- **Retries** with exponential backoff and jitter (the AWS Architecture Blog post explains why jitter matters) for transient errors (timeouts, 5xx, 429); no retry for permanent errors (invalid token, unsubscribed address, malformed number).
- **Dead-letter queues** for messages that exhaust retries, with alerting and replay tooling.
- **Provider failover**: for email and SMS, keep two providers and switch on elevated error rates (a circuit breaker per provider).
- **Feedback loops**: APNs and FCM report invalid tokens; email providers report bounces and complaints. Deactivate tokens and suppress addresses immediately; sending to bad addresses damages sender reputation and deliverability.
- **Push is best effort**: APNs and FCM do not guarantee delivery to the device (offline devices, OS throttling). For anything users must not miss, also write to the in-app inbox.

## Deep dive 5: in-app and real-time
The in-app inbox is a per-user list stored in a database (partitioned by user, sorted by time) plus a live channel (WebSocket or SSE) that pushes a "new notification" event to connected clients. Uber's write-up on its real-time push platform and Netflix's Rapid Event Notification System are good examples of large-scale fan-out to connected devices, including prioritisation and handling clients that reconnect.

## Tracking
Each delivery moves through states (queued, sent, delivered, opened, clicked, failed, suppressed) recorded from worker results and provider webhooks into an append-only log, then aggregated for dashboards (delivery rate per channel, latency p99 per priority, opt-out rate per category). Opt-out rate is the most important product metric: a noisy system trains users to disable notifications entirely.

## Common mistakes
- One queue for everything, so campaigns delay OTPs.
- Sending synchronously from the API request.
- No dedup, or claiming exactly-once.
- Ignoring timezones for quiet hours.
- Not processing provider feedback (dead tokens, bounces).
- Treating push as guaranteed delivery.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** pipeline decomposition, priority isolation, dedup, preference evaluation, provider failure handling and scale for campaigns.

**60-second outline:** scope channels, categories and priorities; ~3k pushes/s steady with campaign spikes; API validates, applies idempotency and enqueues (202); policy workers evaluate preferences, quiet hours, caps and expiry, and expand segments with throttling; render; per-channel, per-priority queues and workers calling providers with backoff, failover and DLQs; dedup keys in Redis; feedback updates tokens and suppression lists; in-app inbox plus live channel; tracking pipeline.

**Follow-ups to expect:** "How do you send 50 million emails without hurting OTP latency?", "How do you implement 'X and 10 others liked your post'?", "How do you schedule a notification for 9 a.m. in each user's timezone?", "What happens if FCM is down for 20 minutes?", "How do you measure whether notifications are helping or annoying users?"
keyPoints: Separate the pipeline into intake, preference and policy evaluation, rendering, per-channel queues and provider workers so each stage scales and fails independently.
Priorities need separate queues (or topics): an OTP or security alert must never wait behind a marketing campaign of 50 million emails.
Dedup with an idempotency key per logical notification (event id + user + channel) stored with a TTL; providers and queues are at-least-once.
Preferences, quiet hours, frequency caps and unsubscribe are evaluated before sending, and some (legal unsubscribe for marketing email) are hard requirements.
Provider calls fail and throttle: retry with exponential backoff and jitter, fail over between providers, and clean up invalid device tokens.
interview: Design a notification system that sends push, email and SMS.
How do you prevent duplicate notifications and respect user preferences?

check.q: Why put transactional notifications (OTP codes, password resets) on a separate queue from marketing campaigns?
options: So a large campaign backlog cannot delay time-critical messages; each priority gets its own capacity and SLO
Queues cannot hold more than one type
check.why: A single FIFO queue makes latency depend on whatever is ahead. Separate queues (and worker pools) isolate priorities so an OTP is sent in seconds even during a 50-million-email campaign.

check.q: A worker sends a push, then crashes before acknowledging the queue message. What prevents a duplicate push on redelivery?
options: Checking a dedup record keyed by notification id and channel, written before or atomically with the send attempt
check.why: Queues redeliver unacknowledged messages. A dedup store (for example Redis SET NX with a TTL) makes the second attempt a no-op. A small window remains if the crash happens between send and record, which is why notifications are effectively at-least-once with best-effort dedup.

check.q: APNs or FCM reports that a device token is no longer valid. What should the system do?
options: Switch to SMS for every future message
Remove or deactivate the token so future sends skip it
check.why: Stale tokens waste capacity and can hurt delivery reputation. Provider feedback should update the device registry immediately.

projects.title: URL shortener at scale: 10k redirects per second with analytics
projects.summary: A production-shaped URL shortener built as a small distributed system: leased-range ID generation, a cached redirect path load-tested to thousands of requests per second, asynchronous click analytics through a log, abuse controls and full observability.
projects.why: Every candidate can describe a URL shortener on a whiteboard; very few have built one and measured it. This project turns the most common system design prompt into evidence: real p99 numbers under load, a cache hit-rate graph, a demonstrated failover of the cache, and an analytics pipeline that never slows the redirect. It gives you concrete numbers and war stories for every follow-up an interviewer can ask.
projects.architecture:
```text
 clients
   |
 load balancer (nginx / envoy)
   |
 +-------------------+--------------------+
 |                   |                    |
 redirect svc x3     api svc (create, stats, takedown)
 | in-proc LRU 5s    |   | token bucket (Redis Lua)
 v                   |   v
 Redis (code -> url, negative cache, rate limits)
 |  miss              |
 v                    v
 Postgres primary + read replica  <-- id range allocator (sequence, blocks of 10k)
 |
 redirect svc --(async, buffered)--> Kafka/Redpanda --> aggregator --> ClickHouse
                                                                        ^
                                              api svc stats queries ----+
 OpenTelemetry collector -> Prometheus / Grafana / Tempo
```

Key decisions: redirects and writes are separate services so the hot path stays tiny and independently scalable. Codes come from leased ranges, so creates need no uniqueness lookup and never collide; a permutation hides ordering. The redirect path never waits on analytics: click events are buffered and dropped (counted) if the broker is unavailable, a deliberate availability-over-completeness choice for analytics.

deepDives.title: Code generation: leased ranges and a permutation
deepDives.body:
Each API instance leases a block of 10,000 ids from a Postgres sequence with `SELECT nextval('link_blocks')`, multiplying by the block size to get its range. Inside the block it mints ids locally with no network call, so creates cost one insert. A crash wastes at most one block, which is irrelevant against a 62^7 (about 3.5 trillion) code space.

Sequential ids would make codes enumerable, so each id passes through a reversible permutation before base62 encoding: a 4-round Feistel network over the id bits with a secret key, or a multiply-by-odd-constant modulo 62^7 with its modular inverse for decoding. Because a permutation is a bijection, uniqueness is preserved and no collision check is needed. Custom aliases live in the same table; generated codes are always exactly 7 characters and aliases must be at least 8 or contain a hyphen, so the two sets can never collide. Compare this in the write-up with random codes (simple, needs unique-constraint retries) and truncated hashes (collisions certain at scale).

deepDives.title: The redirect hot path and hot keys
deepDives.body:
The redirect handler does at most three lookups: an in-process LRU (5 s TTL), Redis, then a Postgres replica. Misses populate both caches, and unknown codes are negatively cached for 60 seconds so scanners cannot hammer the database. A singleflight-style request coalescer ensures a burst of requests for a cold key produces one database read.

Load testing with a Zipf distribution over a million codes shows why each layer exists: Redis alone gives a high hit rate, but a single viral code can push one Redis shard to its limit; the 5 s local cache flattens that to one Redis read per instance per 5 seconds. The trade-off is staleness: a takedown can take up to 5 seconds to apply everywhere, which you mitigate by publishing purge messages on a Redis channel that every instance subscribes to. Record p50, p99 and hit rate before and after each layer; those numbers are the core of your interview story.

deepDives.title: Analytics without touching redirect latency
deepDives.body:
Writing a counter row per click would put a database write on every redirect and create hot rows for viral links. Instead the handler hands a small event (code, timestamp, referrer host, country from GeoIP, user-agent class) to a buffered, non-blocking producer and returns the 302 immediately. If the buffer is full or the broker is down, events are dropped and a counter is incremented, an explicit choice that analytics may lose data during an outage while redirects stay fast.

The consumer aggregates events into one-minute buckets keyed by (code, minute) and writes them to ClickHouse with deterministic bucket keys, using a ReplacingMergeTree or idempotent upserts so replays after a crash do not double count. Offsets are committed only after the bucket write succeeds. The stats API reads pre-aggregated tables for dashboards and raw events for drill-downs. Demonstrate the decoupling in the README: stop the consumer during a load test and show the redirect latency graph does not move.
